paragraphs.text: 1. Here too is something Socrates said to Alcibiades. The young man was in great anxiety and dread of coming forward before the people. Heartening and rousing him, Socrates said, "Do you not despise that cobbler?" naming him. When Alcibiades agreed, Socrates went on, "And what of that man who cries his wares in the markets, or that tent-maker?" When the young man assented, Socrates said, "Well then, the people of the Athenians is gathered together out of such men; and if you despise them one by one, you must despise them when assembled as well." So nobly did the son of Sophroniscus and Phaenarete instruct the son of Cleinias and Deinomache.

2. Once, when Megabyzus was praising poor and unskilful paintings and finding fault with others laboriously and well executed, the boys of Zeuxis who were grinding the ochre laughed at him. Zeuxis therefore said: "While you keep silent, Megabyzus, these boys admire you, for they see your clothing and the attendants about you; but whenever you wish to say something about art, they despise you. Guard yourself, then, among those who are praised, by keeping a hold on your tongue and not playing the connoisseur about matters that are none of your concern."

3. Alexander, when he beheld the portrait of himself at Ephesus painted by Apelles, did not praise it as the work deserved. But when the horse was led in and neighed at the horse in the picture as though at a real and living one, Apelles said: "O king, the horse seems to be a far better judge of painting than you."

4. I wish to tell you of a deed of Phalaris not at all in keeping with his usual character; for the deed proclaims an irresistible humanity, and on that account seems foreign to him. Chariton was a man of Acragas, a lover of beauty and passionately devoted to the bloom of youth; and he loved with the fiercest ardour Melanippus, a man of Acragas, excellent in soul and outstanding in beauty. This Melanippus was wronged in something by Phalaris; for when he was at law with one of the tyrant's own friends, Phalaris ordered him to drop the suit. When he would not obey, the tyrant threatened to do the worst to him if he did not yield. So the friend, by the necessity Phalaris imposed, won the case against justice, and the magistrates destroyed the record of the trial. The young man bore this grievously, saying he had been outraged, and confessed his anger to his lover, and begged him to share in the attack upon the tyrant; and he was eager to take in others among the young men whom he knew to be hottest for such an undertaking. Chariton, seeing him in a frenzy and inflamed with anger, and knowing that none of the citizens would join them for fear of the tyrant, said that he too had long desired this and was zealous by every means to deliver his country from the slavery that had overtaken it; but that it was not safe to make such matters known to many. He asked Melanippus, then, to let him consider these things more carefully, and to allow him to watch for the right moment for the deed. The youth agreed. So Chariton, taking the whole hazard upon himself, and unwilling to take his beloved as a partner — so that, if he were caught, he alone might suffer the penalty and not drag the other into the same — when it seemed to him the time was right, took a dagger and set out against the tyrant. He did not, however, escape notice, for the bodyguards kept watch over such things very strictly. Thrown into prison by Phalaris and racked to make him name his accomplices, he endured it and bore up under the tortures. But when this dragged on, Melanippus came to Phalaris and confessed that he was not only an accomplice of Chariton, but had himself begun the plot. When Phalaris asked the reason, he told the whole story from the beginning and the suppression of the record, and confessed that he had been deeply aggrieved by it. Phalaris, then, marvelling at them both, released them from punishment, ordering them to leave that very day not only the city of Acragas but Sicily itself; yet he allowed them to enjoy their own rightful property. These men the Pythia afterward celebrated, and their love, in these verses: "Guides divine of love to mortal men, blessed were Chariton and Melanippus born" — the god calling their love a divine friendship.

5. The Lacedaemonians practised a remarkable economy of time, husbanding it from every quarter for pressing needs, and allowing none of the citizens either to take their ease or be idle with it, lest, being spent on things outside virtue, it should be wasted to no purpose. A proof of this, among others, is the following. When the ephors of the Lacedaemonians heard that those who had seized Decelea were taking an afternoon walk, they sent word to them: "Do not take walks" — implying that they were living softly rather than training the body. For the Lacedaemonians must procure their health not through walking but through the exercises of the gymnasium.

6. They say that Hippomachus the trainer, when the athlete he was training had managed a certain wrestling-throw, and the whole crowd standing round shouted out, struck him with his rod and said: "But you did badly, and not as you ought, what should have been done better; for these men would not have praised you had you done something skilful" — hinting that those who do each thing well and finely ought to please not the many, but those who have an understanding eye for what is done. Socrates too seems to have made light of the judgement of the many in his conversation with Crito, when Crito came to the prison and tried to persuade him to run away and so frustrate the Athenians' verdict against him.

7. This is a Theban law, rightly and humanely laid down above most: that it is not permitted to a Theban to expose a child or to cast it out into a wilderness, condemning it to death; but if the child's father is poor in the extreme, whether the child be male or female, he is to bring it, fresh from its mother's pains and still in its swaddling-clothes, to the magistrates; and they, receiving the infant, hand it over to whoever offers the smallest price. There is an agreement and a contract with him, that in return he shall rear the child, and when it is grown have it as his slave, male or female, taking its service as the recompense for its upbringing.

8. In the ninety-first Olympiad, in which Exaenetus of Acragas won the foot-race, Xenocles and Euripides competed against each other. And first was Xenocles — whoever he may be — with his Oedipus, Lycaon, Bacchae, and the satyr-play Athamas. Second to him was Euripides with his Alexander, Palamedes, Trojan Women, and the satyr-play Sisyphus. It is absurd — is it not? — that Xenocles should win and Euripides be beaten, and that with such dramas. One of two things, then: either the judges who held the vote were senseless and ignorant and far from a right judgement, or they were bribed. Either is monstrous, and least of all worthy of the Athenians.

9. Consider what the Athenians decreed, and that under a democracy: of the Aeginetans, to cut off the great thumb of the right hand of each, that they might not be able to wield a spear but might pull an oar; of the Mytilenaeans, to slaughter all of military age — this too they decreed, on the proposal of Cleon, son of Cleaenetus. As for the captives taken of the Samians, they were to be branded on the face, and the brand was to be an owl — and this too was an Attic decree. I would not have wished these things either to have been ratified at Athens or to be told of the Athenians — O Athena of the City, and Zeus the Deliverer, and all the gods of the Greeks.

10. I hear of Timotheus, son of Conon, the general of the Athenians, that when he was at the height of his good fortune and was taking the cities with the greatest ease, and the Athenians did not know where to place him out of their wonder at the man — that he, meeting Plato, son of Ariston, walking outside the walls with some of his acquaintances, and seeing him grand to look upon in his breadth, gracious in countenance, and discoursing not about the levying of money nor about triremes, nor about naval needs nor about crews, nor about the necessity of sending help nor about the tribute of the allies, nor about the islanders or any other such trifle, but about those matters of which Plato spoke and was wont to take seriously — the son of Conon, standing still, said: "What a life, and what true happiness!" From this it is plain that Timotheus did not declare himself to be very happy at all, since his happiness lay not in these things, but in his reputation and honour among the Athenians.

11. Socrates, seeing at the beginning of the Thirty the men of distinction put to death and the very wealthy plotted against by the tyrants, is said to have met Antisthenes and said: "Have you any regret that we became nothing great or august in our lives, and not such as we see the monarchs in tragedy — those Atreuses and Thyesteses and Agamemnons and Aegisthuses? For these are exposed to view, slaughtered and made the stuff of tragedy and eating their wicked feasts every time; but no poet of tragedy was ever so bold or shameless as to bring a slaughtered chorus onto the stage in a drama."

12. As for Themistocles, son of Neocles, I do not know whether one should praise this. When Themistocles had ceased from his prodigality — having been disowned by his father — and began to live soberly, and had given up his courtesans, and was seized with another love, the love of the public life of the Athenians, and set himself most ardently to office and was eager to be first, he said, they tell us, to his acquaintances: "What would you give for a man like me, who am not yet envied?" Now one who longs to be envied is striving for that which Euripides calls "being stared at." But that this is empty, the same Euripides declares.

13. Anytus and his party set upon Socrates and plotted against him, for what reasons and on what grounds has been told long ago. But, suspicious of the Athenians and afraid how they would stand toward the accusation of the man — for great was the name of Socrates, both for other reasons and because he refuted the sophists as men with nothing sound about them, who neither knew nor said anything worth the trouble — on these grounds, then, they wished to make trial regarding the slander against him. For they did not think it advisable to bring an indictment against him outright at once, for the reasons I have stated, and for these as well: lest the friends of Socrates, growing savage, should set the judges against them, and they themselves should suffer some incurable harm, as men who falsely accused one who was not only the cause of no evil to the city, but on the contrary an ornament to Athens. What, then, do they devise? They persuade Aristophanes, the comic poet — a buffoon, a man absurd and eager to be so — to make a comedy of Socrates, doubtless the things that go about: that he was a babbler, and that he made the weaker argument appear the stronger, and brought in strange divinities, and neither revered nor honoured the gods, and taught these same things to those who came to him and persuaded them to hold them. Aristophanes, taking a thoroughly bold subject, and sowing in laughter and the charm of his verses, and taking the best of the Greeks for his subject — for the drama was not against Cleon, nor was he making comedy of the Lacedaemonians or Thebans or Pericles himself, but of a man dear to the other gods and especially to Apollo — since, then, it was an unaccustomed thing and a paradoxical spectacle on the stage and in comedy, Socrates, the comedy first of all astonished the Athenians by its unexpectedness; and then, being by nature envious and disposed to begrudge the best — not only those in public life and office, but still more those who were well thought of for fine speech or for the dignity of their lives — they reckoned these Clouds a most delightful entertainment, and applauded the poet as never before, and shouted that he had won, and bade the judges write down Aristophanes above and no other. So much for the drama. As for Socrates, he rarely frequented the theatres; but if ever Euripides, the poet of tragedy, was competing with new tragedies, then he would come. And when Euripides was competing at the Piraeus, Socrates went down there too; for he delighted in the man, both for his wisdom and for his excellence in verse. And once, when Alcibiades, son of Cleinias, and Critias, son of Callaeschrus, were teasing him and forced him to go into the theatre to hear the comedy, he was not pleased with them, but utterly despised — being a man temperate and just and good, and besides wise — men who were mockers and insolent and said nothing sound; which grieved them terribly. So these too were the seeds of the comedy against him, and not only those that are admitted to have come from Anytus and Meletus. It is likely too that Aristophanes was paid for these things. For since they wished — or rather were eager by every means to slander Socrates — and since he himself was poor and accursed, what was strange in his taking money for no good end? But of these things he himself knows; at any rate his drama was well thought of. And indeed it happened then, if ever, as Cratinus says, that the theatre was sick in its wits. And since it was the festival of Dionysus, a very great multitude of the Greeks came in their eagerness for the spectacle. So, when Socrates was being paraded on the stage and named many times — and I would not wonder if he was even seen among the actors, for plainly the mask-makers fashioned him as like as could be — the strangers, who did not know who was being made fun of, raised a murmur and kept asking who this Socrates might be. Perceiving this — for he was present, not idly nor by chance, but knowing they were making a comedy of him, and indeed he sat in a conspicuous place in the theatre — in order to resolve the strangers' perplexity, he stood up and remained standing throughout the whole drama while the actors performed, and so was seen. So far did Socrates carry his disdain of comedy and of the Athenians.

14. That Xerxes was a laughable man, if indeed he despised the sea and the land, the work of Zeus, and made for himself new roads and an unwonted voyage, yet was a slave to a plane-tree and admired the tree. In Lydia, at any rate, they say that, seeing a fine large plane-tree, he stayed there that day with no need to, and used the desert about the tree for his halting-place. Moreover he hung costly ornament upon it, honouring its branches with collars and bracelets, and left a keeper for it, as a guard and warden over a beloved. And from this what good came to the tree? The borrowed adornment, which in no way belonged to it, hung there idly and added nothing to its beauty; since the beauty of a tree is this — noble branches, abundant foliage, a firm trunk, deep roots, winds that toss it, far-spreading shade from it, the seasons turning, and water, some nourishing it through channels, some watering it from heaven; but Xerxes' robes and the barbarian's gold and the rest of the gifts were worthy neither of the plane-tree nor of any other noble tree.

15. Some men of Clazomenae, coming to Sparta and behaving with insolence and arrogance, smeared with soot the thrones of the ephors, where they are accustomed to sit and conduct business and arrange each of the city's affairs. When the ephors learned of it, they were not angry, but, summoning the public herald, ordered him to proclaim publicly this admired pronouncement: "Let it be permitted to the Clazomenians to behave indecently."

16. This too of Phocion, son of Phocus, I know to be a fine thing. Coming forward before the Athenians at an assembly, when he had some reproach to make against them for their folly, he said, very wisely and tellingly: "I had rather suffer some harm at your hands than myself do you any harm."

17. The wisdom of the Magi among the Persians knows, among the other things it is permitted them to know, also how to prophesy. These men foretold the savagery and bloodthirstiness of Ochus toward his subjects, having discerned it through certain secret signs. For when, upon the death of his father Artaxerxes, Ochus came to the kingship of the Persians, the Magi ordered one of the eunuchs standing near to watch which of the dishes set before him Ochus would attack first, when the table was laid. And while the eunuch stood watching this, Ochus stretched out his hands, took with his right one of the knives lying by, and with the other drew toward him the largest of the loaves, and laying meat upon it, then cut and ate without stint. Hearing this, the Magi prophesied these two things: abundance from the seasons and good harvests during the time of his reign, and many murders. And they were not deceived.

18. Timotheus, son of Conon, the general of the Athenians, once, having withdrawn from those costly dinners and those generals' banquets, was taken by Plato to the symposium in the Academy and entertained simply and after the manner of the Muses; and returning home he said to his household that those who dine with Plato are well even on the morrow. From this Timotheus disparaged costly and vulgar dinners as not pleasing at all on the day after. There is another story, brother to the one just told and meaning the same thing, though not telling it in the same words, that goes about: that on the next day Timotheus, meeting Plato, said: "You, Plato, dine better for the morrow than for the present day."

19. Alexander, when he had conquered Darius and gained the empire of the Persians, thinking great things of himself and made a god by the good fortune that had then encompassed him, sent word to the Greeks to vote him a god. Absurdly. For what nature had not given him, this he gained nothing by demanding from men. So various peoples voted various things, but the Lacedaemonians voted this: "Since Alexander wishes to be a god, let him be a god" — thus in their laconic and native fashion the Lacedaemonians convicting Alexander of folly.

20. They say that King Antigonus was of the people and gentle. Whoever has leisure to know the particulars about him and to examine each detail of the man will learn them elsewhere; but I will tell what I am about to say, which is very gentle and unassuming of him. This Antigonus, seeing his son treat his subjects too violently and too boldly, said: "Do you not know, my son, that our kingship is a glorious slavery?" Now Antigonus's words to his son are very mild and humane; but if anyone thinks otherwise, then that man, it seems to me, does not know a kingly or statesmanlike person, but is rather suited to living with a tyrant.

21. Pausanias of the deme Ceramus loved the poet Agathon. This is much talked of; but what has not gone out to all, I will tell. They once came to the court of Archelaus, this lover and his beloved. Now Archelaus was no less amorous than fond of the Muses. Since, then, he often saw Pausanias and Agathon quarrelling with each other, thinking that the lover was being slighted by his favourite, Archelaus asked Agathon what he meant by so frequently falling out with the man who loved him above all. And Agathon said: "I will tell you, king. For I am neither quarrelsome toward him, nor do I do this out of boorishness; but if I too understand anything of human character, both otherwise and from poetry, I find it most pleasant for lovers to be reconciled with their beloveds after a quarrel, and I am convinced that nothing so delightful befalls them. So I often give him a share of this pleasure by quarrelling with him repeatedly; for he rejoices whenever I am continually ending my quarrel with him, whereas if I approached him evenly and as a matter of habit he would not know the difference." Archelaus, the story goes, praised this. They say too that the poet Euripides also loved this same Agathon, and that he composed his drama Chrysippus as a favour to him. Whether this is certain I cannot declare; but I know that it is said by most.

22. I hear that the Mantineans too were among the best-governed peoples, no less than the Locrians or the Cretans or the Lacedaemonians themselves or the Athenians; for a grand thing too was the work of Solon, even if afterward the Athenians little by little corrupted some of the laws he had written for them.

23. Nicodorus the boxer, having been among the most renowned of the Mantineans, late in his life and after his athletic career became their lawgiver, and so governed his country far better than by his proclamations in the stadiums. They say that Diagoras of Melos, who was his lover, composed the laws for him. I had something further to say about Nicodorus; but lest I should seem to be also taking up the praise of Diagoras, let my account go only so far. For Diagoras was hateful to the gods, and it is no pleasure to me to make much mention of him.

24. Some have already cast down the famous strength of Milo of Croton, telling such things about him. The pomegranate of this Milo, which he held in his hand, none of his opponents could pull out; but his beloved drew it out very easily, contending with him often. From this one may understand that Milo was strong in body, but not brave in soul.

25. They say that the sixth of the month Thargelion was the cause of many good things, not only to the Athenians but to many others as well. For instance, Socrates was born on this day; and the Persians were defeated on this day; and the Athenians sacrifice to Artemis Agrotera the three hundred she-goats, doing this in accordance with the vow of Miltiades. On the sixth of the same month they say too that the battle of Plataea took place and that the Greeks were victorious; for their earlier defeat, which I mentioned, occurred at Artemisium. And the victory of the Greeks at Mycale is agreed to have been the gift of no other day than this, since on the same day they were victorious both at Plataea and at Mycale. And Alexander the Macedonian, the son of Philip, they say destroyed the many myriads of the barbarians on the sixth too, when Alexander overthrew Darius. And all agree it was in the same month. And Alexander himself is believed both to have been born and to have departed from life on the same day.

26. Aristotle says that by the Crotoniates Pythagoras was called Hyperborean Apollo. And the son of Nicomachus adds this too, that once on the same day and at the same hour he was seen by many both at Metapontum and at Croton, rising up at the games, where Pythagoras also revealed that one of his thighs was of gold. The same writer says too that as he was crossing the river Cosas he was addressed by it; and he says that many heard this address.

27. Anniceris of Cyrene prided himself greatly on horsemanship and the driving of chariots. And so once he wished to display his skill to Plato. Yoking his chariot, he drove many courses round the Academy, keeping so exactly to the line of the course that he did not stray beyond the wheel-tracks, but always went along them. Now all the rest, as was natural, were astonished; but Plato found fault with his excessive zeal, saying: "It is impossible for one who lays out so much care upon things so small and worthless to be in earnest about anything great; for, all his thought being given over to those things, he must necessarily neglect what truly deserves to be admired."

28. After the victory over the Persians the Athenians established a law that cocks should fight publicly in the theatre one day of the year. Whence this law took its beginning I will tell. When Themistocles was leading out the citizen force against the barbarians, he saw cocks fighting; and he did not look on idly, but halted the army and said to them: "These birds suffer hardship neither for their country nor for their fathers' gods nor for the tombs of their ancestors, nor for glory nor for freedom nor for their young, but only that neither may be beaten and neither yield to the other." Having said this, he strengthened the Athenians. So the watchword that then arose for them he wished to preserve as an incitement to valour and a reminder for like deeds.

29. Pittacus at Mytilene set up in the temples ladders fit for no use, but to be dedications for this very purpose, hinting at the shifting of fortune up and down — how, in a manner, the fortunate go up and the unfortunate come down.

30. Plato, son of Ariston, at first set out for poetry, and wrote heroic verses; then he burned them, despising them, when, comparing them with Homer's, he saw them far inferior. So he turned to tragedy, and indeed composed a tetralogy, and was about to compete, having already given the poems to the actors. But before the festival of Dionysus he came and heard Socrates, and once caught by that man's Siren, he not only withdrew then from the contest, but utterly cast away the writing of tragedy, and stripped himself for philosophy.

31. And who would not praise the wisdom of the barbarians? Seeing that none of them fell into atheism, nor do they doubt about the gods whether they exist or not, or whether they care for us or not. None of them, at any rate, conceived such a notion as Euhemerus of Messene, or Diogenes the Phrygian, or Hippon, or Diagoras, or Sosias, or Epicurus — no Indian or Celt or Egyptian. Rather, the aforesaid barbarians say both that there are gods and that they have forethought for us and signify beforehand things to come, through birds and through omens and through entrails and through certain other lessons and teachings — which are instructive to men, coming from the gods' forethought toward them. And they say too that many things are foreshown through dreams and through the stars themselves. And, having a strong belief about these matters, they sacrifice in purity and keep themselves holy and pure, and perform rites and observe the law of the mysteries, and do the other things from which it is agreed that they strongly revere and honour the gods.

32. Certain Pythian accounts say that Heracles, the son of Zeus and Alcmene, was from birth called Alcaeus, but that later, coming to Delphi for some reason to seek an oracle, he not only did not fail of the things for which he had come, but heard besides, privately from the god, these words: "Phoebus names you Heracles for your surname; for, bringing glory to men, you shall have undying fame."

33. We see the nature of rivers and their streams; yet those who honour them and make their images, some set them up in human form, while others gave them the shape of bulls. To bulls, then, the Stymphalians liken the Erasinus and the Metope, the Lacedaemonians the Eurotas, the Sicyonians and Phliasians the Asopus, the Argives the Cephisus; in the form of men, the Psophidians honour the Erymanthus, the Heraeans the Alpheus, and the Chersonesians from Cnidus likewise honour the same river in the same way. The Athenians represent the Cephisus as a man in profile, with horns just showing. And in Sicily the Syracusans likened the Anapus to a man, but honoured the spring Cyane with the image of a woman; the Egestaeans honour the Porpax and the Crimisus and the Telmessus in the form of men. The people of Acragas, likening the river that gives its name to the city to a youth in his bloom, sacrifice to it. These same people also dedicated at Delphi a statue carved of ivory, and inscribed on it the name of the river. And the statue is of a boy.

34. They say that Epicharmus, being very old indeed, sitting with some men of his own age in a club-room, when each of those present said — one, "Five years is enough for me to live," another, "Three for me," and a third said, "Four for me" — Epicharmus broke in and said: "My good friends, why do you wrangle and dispute over a few days? For all of us who are gathered here are, by some chance, at our setting; so it is time for all of us to be off as quickly as possible, before any of us comes to suffer some evil of old age."

35. Gorgias of Leontini, being at the end of his life and very aged, was seized by some weakness, and lay slipping little by little into sleep. When one of his friends came to look in on him and asked how he did, Gorgias answered: "Now sleep is beginning to hand me over to his brother."

36. Socrates too, being very far advanced in age and then falling sick, when someone asked him how he was, said: "Well, as regards either outcome; for if I live, I shall have the more to envy me, and if I die, the more to praise me."

37. Of Zaleucus the Locrian there are many other laws too, laid down most finely and as need required, and this not least. If any of the Epizephyrian Locrians, being ill, drank unmixed wine without the physician's prescribing it, even if he recovered, death was his penalty, because he drank what had not been prescribed to him.

38. This too is a Massiliot law: that women should have nothing to do with wine, but that women of every age should drink water. Theophrastus says that this law is in force among the Milesians too, and that the women of Miletus obey it. And why should I not tell the Roman law too? And how should I not justly be charged with unreason, if I have set down in memory the laws of the Locrians and the Massiliots and the Milesians, but leave aside those of my own country? Among the Romans, then, this law was in force above all others. Neither a free woman nor a serving-woman would drink wine, nor would those of good birth who were in their youth, up to thirty-five years of age.

39. The Cretans bade their freeborn children learn the laws to a kind of melody, that they might be charmed by the music and take them more easily into memory, and that, if they should do anything forbidden, they might not have the excuse of having acted in ignorance. As a second lesson they appointed them to learn the hymns of the gods; as a third, the encomia of good men.

40. Everything irrational is by nature ill-disposed toward wine, and especially those animals which become drunk when overfilled with husks or grape-stones. Ravens too, when they eat the herb called oenutta, and dogs themselves as well, become frenzied. And if an ape and an elephant drink wine, the elephant forgets its strength, the ape its cunning; and they are very easily caught.

41. Lovers of drink are said to have been Dionysius the tyrant of Sicily, and Nysaeus, who was also a tyrant, and Apollocrates the son of Dionysius the tyrant, and Hipparinus, son of Dionysius, and Timolaus the Theban, and Charidemus of Oreus, and Arcadion, and Erasixenus, and Alcetas the Macedonian, and Diotimus the Athenian. This last was even nicknamed "the Funnel"; for, putting a funnel into his mouth, he would let the wine poured in pass down without ceasing. Cleomenes the Lacedaemonian they say was not only a great drinker, but they ascribe to him besides that Scythian vice, that he became a drinker of unmixed wine. And Ion of Chios, the poet, they say was himself intemperate about wine. And Alexander the Macedonian, in honour of Calanus the Brahman, the Indian sage, when that man burned himself, held a contest of music and horsemen and athletes. And, gratifying the Indians, he reckoned in among the prizes mentioned a contest native to them, in honour of Calanus. He set up a contest of wine-drinking, and the prize for the one who came first was a talent, for the second thirty minae, and for the third ten. The one who bound on the crown of victory among them was Promachus. And under Dionysius, at the festival of the Pitchers, a golden crown was set as a prize for whoever drank most. And Xenocrates of Chalcedon won, and taking the crown, when he was returning after the dinner, he set it upon the Hermes standing before the doors, according to the custom of the days before; for he laid up and left there the garlands of flowers and of myrtle and of ivy and of bay as well. And Anacharsis too, they say, drank a great deal at Periander's, bringing this provision with him from home; for it is characteristic of the Scythians to drink unmixed wine. And Lacydes and Timon the philosophers, these too they say drank a great deal. And Mycerinus the Egyptian, when the oracle from Buto came to him foretelling the shortness of his life, then wished to outwit the prophecy, doubling the time and adding the nights to the days, and continued himself sleepless and drinking at once. Set down with these also Amasis the Egyptian, if Herodotus is sufficient to bear witness for anyone. And Nicoteles the Corinthian must not be left out of these, nor Scopas, son of Creon. And King Antiochus they say was a lover of wine; for which reason Aristus and Themison the Cyprians governed the kingdom for him, while he, through his hard drinking, held the rule only in name. And Antiochus surnamed Epiphanes, who was given to the Romans as a hostage, he too thirsted intemperately to drink wine. And his namesake Antiochus, who in Media made war on Arsaces, he too was a slave to drink. And Antiochus called the Great, let him too be ranked with these. And Agron, king of the Illyrians, the unjust craving for wine killed, and worked pleurisy in him. And another king of the Illyrians, Gentius, he too was used to drink intemperately. As for Orophernes, king of the Cappadocians, shall we leave him out, who also became a terrible drinker? And if one must mention women too — a woman fond of drink is monstrous, and one given to much drinking still more so, but let it be said of these too. Cleo, they say, entering into contest not with women only but with the men who were her fellow-drinkers, was most formidable at drinking, and overcame them all, carrying off, in my judgement, a most shameful prize of victory.

42. The reputation of Plato and the report of the virtue that was his reached even the Arcadians and the Thebans, and so they entreated him, sending ambassadors with the utmost earnestness, that the man should come to them — not merely for the oversight of their young men, nor that he might join them in philosophical discussion, but, what is still greater than these, they called him to be their lawgiver. They were not, then, likely to fail of the man; for the son of Ariston was pleased at the invitation, and was indeed going to comply. He asked, however, of those who had come, how they stood toward all having an equal share. But when he learned from them that they were quite ill-disposed to it, and that he would not persuade them to honour equality before the law, he refused to visit them.

43. The poorest of men were the best of the Greeks: Aristides, son of Lysimachus, and Phocion, son of Phocus, and Epaminondas, son of Polymnis, and Pelopidas the Theban, and Lamachus the Athenian, and Socrates, son of Sophroniscus, and Ephialtes, son of Sophonides, he too.

44. Of Theon the painter many other works besides attest that his craftsmanship was good, and so too does this picture. There is a hoplite rushing to the rescue, the enemy having suddenly burst in and at once laying waste and ravaging the land; vividly and most ardently the young man seems like one hurrying into battle, and you would say he was inspired, as though driven mad by Ares. His eyes look fierce, and snatching up his arms he seems to dart against the enemy as fast as his feet can carry him. From here he already thrusts forward his shield, and brandishes his bared sword, looking like one bent on bloodshed and gazing on slaughter, and threatening through his whole bearing that he will spare none. And Theon laboured at nothing more — no file-leader, no captain, no centurion, no horseman, no archer — but this single hoplite was enough for him to fulfil the demand of the picture. The artist, however, did not uncover the painting nor show it to those gathered for the viewing before he set a trumpeter beside it and ordered him to blow the rousing strain, piercing and as loud as could be, and such as wakens men to battle. So at the same moment the strain was heard, harsh and fearful, such as trumpets sound for the sally of hoplites swiftly rushing to the rescue, and the painting was uncovered, and the soldier was seen, the strain making the image of the man rushing to the rescue still more vivid to the mind.

1. Socrates used to speak of the divine sign that accompanied him to Theages and Demodocus and to many others. He said that often, by a heavenly dispensation, a voice came to him; "and whenever it comes," he said, "it always signals to me a turning-away from what I am about to do, but it never urges me on. And again, if one of my friends consults me about something, and that voice comes, once more it turns me away. In this way it advises me, and I in turn advise the one who consults me; and I do not let him act, following the divine forewarning." He offered as a witness Charmides the son of Glaucon: for Charmides told him that he intended to train for the foot-race at Nemea, and the moment he began to speak the voice came. Socrates tried to keep Charmides from holding to his purpose, but Charmides was not persuaded; and indeed his effort did not come out as it should.

2. Hipparchus, the eldest of the sons of Pisistratus, was the wisest of the Athenians. He was the first to bring the verses of Homer to Athens, and he compelled the rhapsodes to sing them at the Panathenaea. He also sent a fifty-oared ship to fetch Anacreon of Teos to him. And Simonides of Ceos he kept always near him with great eagerness, winning him over, as one would expect, with great gifts and fees; for that Simonides was fond of money, no one will deny. The care of educated men was indeed this Hipparchus's chief concern. He wished the Athenians to be educated under his own patronage, and he was eager to rule over them while they grew better men; for he thought one ought to envy no man his wisdom, being himself a man of nobility and worth. So Plato says, if indeed the Hipparchus is truly Plato's.

3. There is this Attic custom: when the ox has been slaughtered, they acquit all the others, judging each in turn for the killing; but they condemn the knife, and say that it killed the animal. And the day on which they do this they call the festival of the Dipolia, and also the Bouphonia.

4. They say that Poliarchus the Athenian went so far in luxury that he had even those dogs and cocks in which he delighted carried out to public burial when they died. He invited his friends to their funeral, buried them lavishly, and set up monuments over them, carving epitaphs upon them.

5. Neleus son of Codrus, having no share in the kingship, left Athens because the Pythia had bestowed the rule on Medon; and he set out to found a colony. He put in at Naxos, not by choice but forced by a storm; and when he wished to sail away, contrary winds blowing against him prevented him. As he was at a loss what to do in his straits, the seers said that the camp must be purified, since many sailed with him whose hands were not clean. So he himself pretended to have killed a child and to need purification; and he withdrew, and persuaded the others who shared the same guilt to do likewise. When this had happened and those men had been found out, he abandoned them, and they settled Naxos. But Neleus came to Ionia, and first founded Miletus, having driven out the Carians and the Mygdonians and the Leleges and other barbarians, from whom the twelve cities in Ionia took their name. These are they: Miletus, Ephesus, Erythrae, Clazomenae, Priene, Lebedos, Teos, Colophon, Myus, Phocaea, Samos, and Chios. And later he founded many other cities on the mainland.

6. They say that none of the ancient Thracians knew letters; indeed all the barbarians who dwell in Europe held it most shameful to use writing. But those in Asia, as the story goes, used them more. Hence some even dare to say that Orpheus, being a Thracian, was no wise man, but that the legends about him are otherwise false. This Androtion says, if anyone is to be trusted on the illiteracy and want of culture of the Thracians.

7. When Alexander took Darius, he held a wedding feast for himself and for his companions. The bridegrooms were ninety, and the bridal chambers equal in number to them. The hall that received and entertained them held a hundred couches; and each couch had silver feet, but his own had golden feet, and all were adorned with purple and embroidered coverings of barbarian weave, very costly. He also brought into the banquet his personal guest-friends, and seated them facing himself. In the courtyard the other forces feasted, the infantry and the navy and the cavalry, and the embassies too and the Greeks who were visiting. The meals were held to the trumpet: it sounded the assembling note when they were to come in to the feast, and the recall note when it signalled them to depart. For five days running he celebrated the weddings with sacrifices. Musicians and actors came too, some of comedy and some of tragedy, very many of them. There were also from India conjurers of distinction, and they were thought to surpass all the others from elsewhere.

8. Cimon of Cleonae, they say, perfected the art of painting while it was still in its infancy and was being practised without skill and without experience by those before him, in a manner still, so to speak, in swaddling-clothes and at the breast. For this reason he was the first to receive larger fees than his predecessors.

9. Archelaus the tyrant of the Macedonians — for so Plato names him, and not "king" — had a favourite, Crateuas, who fell in love with the tyranny no less than Archelaus had loved the boy, and he killed his lover, expecting that he would become a tyrant and a man of fortune. But having held the tyranny three or four days, he in turn was plotted against by others and met his end. It would be most fitting to apply to this Macedonian drama that verse: "He who contrives evil for another contrives it for his own heart." They say that Archelaus had broken faith with him, having promised to give him one of his daughters; and when he married the girl to another, Crateuas in his rage destroyed Archelaus.

10. The Athenians chose Solon to rule them by election, for they did not choose him by lot. When he had been chosen, he set the city in order in other respects, and in particular he drew up for them the laws that are still kept to this day. And then the Athenians ceased to use the laws of Draco; those laws were called "ordinances." Only his homicide laws did they keep.

11. We shall no longer wonder if human nature, being mortal and short-lived, compels men to perish, when we see even rivers failing, and hear that even the highest of the mountains are diminishing. The voyagers, at any rate, say that Etna is seen to be smaller than it was before; and they say that Parnassus and Pierian Olympus have suffered the same thing. And those who think they have observed the nature of the universe still more closely say that even the cosmos itself is perishing.

12. Strange, is it not? Yet true. When Demosthenes failed in Macedonia, Aeschines son of Atrometus, of the deme Cothocidae, both stood in high repute with the Macedonians and far surpassed the other envoys in spirit. The cause of this for Aeschines was his friendship with Philip and the gifts he had from him, and the fact that Philip listened to him gently and gladly, regarding him with a kindly look and showing the goodwill he bore him. All this drew Aeschines on to free speech and to a ready flow of words. Demosthenes was not the only one to suffer this in Macedonia, clever as he was at speaking; Theophrastus of Eresus did the same. For he too broke down while speaking before the Council of the Areopagus, and offered this excuse, that he had been overawed by the dignity of the council. Most bitterly and most readily, then, did Demochares meet this speech of his, saying: "Theophrastus, they were Athenians who sat in judgment, not the twelve gods."
13. They say that Anaxagoras of Clazomenae was never seen laughing, nor smiling at all. They say too that Aristoxenus was a mighty enemy of laughter; and that Heraclitus wept over everything in life.

14. Diogenes of Sinope, when at last he lay sick unto death, dragged himself along alone and threw himself down beside a little bridge near a gymnasium, and ordered the keeper of the wrestling-school, when he perceived that he had breathed his last, to throw him into the Ilissus. So little did Diogenes care for either death or burial.

15. When Philip conquered the Athenians at Chaeronea, though elated by his success, he nonetheless kept his reason in check and did not grow insolent; and for this reason he thought he ought to be reminded each morning by one of his pages that he was a man, and he gave the boy this duty to perform. And they say that he would neither go out himself, nor would any of those who had business with him be admitted to him, until the boy had called this out to him three times.

16. Solon son of Execestides, being now an old man, suspected that Pisistratus would set himself up as tyrant, when Pisistratus came forward in the assembly of the Athenians and asked for a bodyguard. Seeing that the Athenians listened carelessly to his own words but gave heed to Pisistratus, he said that he was wiser than some and braver than others: than those who do not understand that, once he has obtained a guard for his person, he will be tyrant — wiser than these; and than those who understand it yet keep silent — braver than these. But Pisistratus, having received the force, was tyrant. Then Solon, sitting before his house with his shield and spear laid beside him, said that he had armed himself and was aiding his country as he could, being no longer a general because of his age, but loyal in his judgment. Yet Pisistratus, whether out of respect for the man and his wisdom, or out of remembrance of their youth — for the man is said to have been his favourite — did Solon no harm at all. And so Solon, a little later, being very old, ended his life, leaving behind a great reputation for wisdom and courage. They set up a bronze statue of him in the marketplace, and they buried him too at public expense beside the gates near the wall, on the right as one enters, and his tomb was walled about.

17. Scythes of Inycum, the sole ruler of the Zanclaeans, went up into Asia to King Darius. And Darius judged him the most just of all the men who had come up to him from Greece, because, having asked the king's leave, he went to Sicily and from Sicily back again to the king. This Democedes of Croton did not do, and for this reason Darius spoke ill of him, calling him a cheat and a most worthless man. So Scythes, living in great prosperity among the Persians, ended his life in old age.

18. Euthymus the Locrian, of those in Italy, was a good boxer, and he is believed to have been most marvellous in bodily strength; for the Locrians show a stone of the greatest size, which he carried and set before his doors. And the hero in Temesa, who was exacting tribute from the neighbouring people, he made to cease; for, coming to the hero's shrine, which was forbidden ground to most men, he fought it out with him, and forced him to pay back more than he had plundered. From this, indeed, the proverb spread, said of those who profit by something to no good end, that "the hero in Temesa will come to them." They say that this same Euthymus, going down to the river Caecinus, which is before the city of the Locrians, vanished.

19. This is the epitaph inscribed for Anaxagoras: "Here, having passed to the utmost bound of truth concerning the heavenly cosmos, lies Anaxagoras." And there is an altar set up to him, and on it is inscribed by some "To Mind," by others "To Truth."

1. Aspasia, the daughter of Hermotimus, the Phocaean, was reared in orphanhood, her mother having died in childbirth. So Aspasia was brought up in poverty, yet temperately and with endurance. A dream came to her often and foretold good things, hinting at her future fortune, that she would live with a man of nobility and worth. While she was still a child, there appeared on her face, just below the chin, a tumour, ugly to see, and it grieved both her father and the girl. So her father showed her to a physician; and he promised to heal it if he received three staters. The father said he had not the money, and the physician said that he himself had no remedy at hand. Aspasia was distressed, as was natural, at this, and going out of doors she wept; and holding a mirror on her knees and seeing herself in it, she was greatly pained. As she had eaten no dinner because of her grief, a very timely sleep came upon her, and with the sleep a dove appeared, and turning into a woman it said: "Take heart, and bid a long farewell to physicians and their remedies; take of the rose-garlands of Aphrodite, however dry they may now be, and rubbing them fine sprinkle them on the tumour." When the girl had heard this and done it, the tumour vanished; and Aspasia was again the fairest of her companions, having received back her beauty from the fairest of the goddesses. And she had an abundance of graces, as no other maiden of that time; her hair was golden and lightly curling, her eyes were very large, her nose a little hooked, and her ears very small. Her skin was tender, and the colour of her face was like roses. For this reason the Phocaeans, while she was still a child, called her Milto. Her lips too showed red, and her teeth were whiter than snow. Her ankles were fine, of the kind that Homer, in his own speech, gives to the most beautiful women, calling them "fair-ankled." Her voice was sweet and tender: one would have said, hearing her speak, that he was hearing a Siren. From all the busyness and fussiness of women she was free. For wealth tends to supply such things; but she, being poor and reared by a father who was himself poor, contributed nothing fussy or superfluous to her appearance. Now Aspasia once came to Cyrus, the son of Darius and Parysatis, the brother of Artaxerxes — not willingly, nor with her father's consent, but by force, such as often befalls when cities are captured or tyrants or satraps use violence. One of Cyrus's satraps, then, brought her up to Cyrus along with other maidens, and very quickly she was preferred above the other concubines for the simplicity of her character and the modesty of her manner and because she was beautiful without artifice. There helped her too, toward being loved beyond measure, the fact that she had understanding. Often, indeed, Cyrus used her as an adviser even in pressing matters, and when persuaded he did not repent of it. When Aspasia first came to Cyrus, he happened to have just risen from dinner and was about to drink in the Persian manner; for after they have eaten their fill, the Persians give themselves up zealously to wine and to toasts, as though stripping for a contest with the drink as their rival. In the middle of the drinking, then, four Greek maidens were brought before Cyrus, among them Aspasia of Phocaea. They were most finely got up; for three of them had had their hair plaited and their faces painted with cosmetics and pigments by their own attendant women, who happened to have come up with them. They had also been taught by their nurses how they must approach Cyrus and how to flatter him, and not to turn away when he came near, nor to be displeased at his touch, nor to refuse his kiss — courtesan's lessons indeed, and the practices of women who trade hucksterishly on their beauty. So they vied with one another to surpass each other in beauty. But Aspasia would not put on a costly tunic, nor consented to wrap herself in an embroidered robe, nor would she submit to bathe, but calling on all the Greek and Liberating gods, she cried aloud her father's name, and cursed herself and her father, believing that the dress and elaborate adornment of her body, contrary to her habit, was a plain and confessed slavery. When struck, she put it on by compulsion, and yielded to the orders, grieving nonetheless that she was forced to do not maidenly but courtesan's things. So the others, coming forward, looked Cyrus in the face and smiled and assumed a cheerful air; but Aspasia looked down, and her face was filled with deep flushes of fiery red, and her eyes brimmed with tears, and in every way she was plainly ashamed. When he bade the women sit near him, the rest obeyed quite readily, but the Phocaean paid no heed to the command, until the satrap who had brought her sat her down by force. And when Cyrus touched them and examined their eyes and their cheeks and their fingers, the others bore it, but she would not endure it; for when Cyrus merely touched her with the tip of his hand, she cried out and said he would weep for doing such things. Cyrus was greatly delighted at this. And when she rose up and tried to flee, because he had touched her breasts, then indeed the son of Darius admired her nobility in a manner not Persian, and looking at the man who had bought her he said: "This one alone you have brought me free and undefiled; the rest are hucksterish both in appearance and still more in manner." From this Cyrus loved her more than any human being with whom he had ever consorted. Some time later Cyrus was deeply in love with her, and was loved in return by her, and their love advanced to such a point that it was near to equality of honour, and not out of tune with the concord and temperance of a Greek marriage. So the fame of his love for Aspasia spread even to Ionia and to all Greece. The Peloponnese too was filled with talk about Cyrus and her, and the report came even to the Great King; for it was believed that Cyrus, after her, would not deign to make trial of any other woman. From this there came back to Aspasia the memory of the old visions, of that dove and of its words and of all that the goddess had foretold; and she believed that the goddess had been her guardian from the beginning, and she offered to Aphrodite rites of initiation and thank-offerings. First, then, she had an image of gold made for her, of sufficient size. She supposed this image to be Aphrodite, and she set beside it a dove studded with jewels; and every day she propitiated the goddess with sacrifices and words of good omen. She sent also to her father Hermotimus many fine gifts, and made him rich. And she lived in temperance, as the Greek and Persian women say. A necklace was once brought to Cyrus from Thessaly, the younger Scopas having sent it; and the gift had been brought to Scopas from Sicily, and the necklace seemed wrought with marvellous art and intricacy. So when all to whom Cyrus showed it were full of wonder, he, greatly pleased with the treasure, went at once to Aspasia's, at midday, and finding her asleep, he slipped under her cloak and lay quietly beside her, and waited without a sound, keeping still himself; and she slept on. When she awoke and saw Cyrus, she embraced him in her wonted way and showed him affection. He, taking the necklace from its little box, showed it, saying that it was worthy either of a king's daughter or of a king's mother. When she agreed, he said: "See, then, I give it to you to have as your own; and put it on, as you are, and show me your neck." But she was not overcome by the gift, but answered very wisely and learnedly: "And how," she said, "shall I dare to put on myself a gift worthy of Parysatis, your mother? Rather send it to her, Cyrus; and I will provide you a fair neck even without it." So Aspasia, high-mindedly and in a manner royal beyond what women do, acted the opposite of what women are wont to do; for they are terribly fond of finery. But Cyrus, pleased with the answer, kissed Aspasia, and writing down each thing that had been done and said in a letter, he sent it to his mother together with the necklace. And Parysatis, receiving the gift, was no less pleased with what was written than with the gold; and in return for this she rewarded Aspasia with great and royal gifts. For this above all delighted her, that although Aspasia stood in very high favour with her son, yet in being loved by Cyrus she wished to be surpassed by Cyrus's mother. So Aspasia praised the gifts, but said she did not need them, since money too had come to her with the gifts, very much of it; and she sent it to Cyrus, saying: "To you, who feed many men, this might be useful; but to me you suffice, being loved, and you are my adornment." By this, as was natural, she astonished Cyrus, and beyond dispute this woman was admired both for the beauty of her body and still more for the nobility of her soul. When Cyrus was killed in the battle against his brother, and Cyrus's camp was taken, she too was captured along with the other spoils — not falling into the enemy's hands at random and by chance, but King Artaxerxes sought her out with much care; for he knew her fame and her excellence. When they brought her to him in bonds, he was indignant, and threw those who had done this into prison, and ordered that costly adornment be given her. But she, unwilling and lamenting and weeping over many things, was forced to put on the king's dress; for she mourned bitterly for Cyrus. Having put it on, she appeared the fairest of women, and at once Artaxerxes was inflamed and consumed, and held her first of his women, and honoured her beyond measure by his eagerness to please her, trusting that he would persuade her to forget Cyrus and would teach her to love him no less than that man. And he attained his hope, but late and slowly; for the goodwill toward Cyrus that had melted into Aspasia had wrought in her, more than anything, a love-charm hard to wash away. Some time later Tiridates the eunuch died, the fairest and most beautiful youth in Asia; he ended his life while still in his bloom and just emerging from boyhood, and the king was said to love him most ardently. From this the king mourned most grievously and grieved most bitterly, and there was public mourning throughout all Asia, all men gratifying the king in this. And no one dared approach him or console him; for they believed that he was incurably affected by what had happened. When three days had passed, Aspasia, putting on a mourning dress, as the king was going off to his bath, stood weeping and looking at the ground; and he, seeing her, was astonished and asked the reason of her coming. And she said: "I have come, O king, to console you in your grief and pain, if it is your wish; but if you are angry, I will go back again." The Persian was greatly pleased at her care, and bade her go up to the chamber and await him; and she did so. When he returned, he put the eunuch's robe over Aspasia's black dress; and somehow the youth's garb suited her, and her beauty shone out all the more to her lover. When once he was won over by this, he begged her, until the keenness of his grief should fade, to come to him dressed thus. And she, to please him, was persuaded; and she alone of all in Asia — not of the women only, they say, but of the king's sons and kinsmen — consoled Artaxerxes and healed the affliction of his grief, the king yielding to her care and wisely persuaded by her consolation.

3. Epaminondas, when he was mortally wounded at Mantinea, was carried to his tent still breathing, and called for Daiphantus, that he might appoint him general; but they said the man was dead. Then he asked that Iolaidas be called quickly. When he too was said to be dead, he advised them to make terms with the enemy and form a friendship, since no general was left in Thebes.
4. The Egyptians say that Sesostris was instructed in the laws by Hermes.
5. Lais the courtesan, as Aristophanes of Byzantium says, was also called "the Axe." This surname convicted her of the savagery of her character.

6. One may laugh at those who are proud because of their fathers, seeing that among the Romans we do not know the father of Marius, yet we admire him for his deeds; and of Cato the Elder too the father must be sought out.
7. Alexander crowned the tomb of Achilles, and Hephaestion that of Patroclus, hinting that he too was the beloved of Alexander, as Patroclus was of Achilles.

8. Cleomenes the Laconian, taking Archonides as a partner from among his companions, made him a sharer in his affairs. So he swore that, if he gained power, he would do everything with his head. Having gained the rule, then, he killed his companion and cut off his head and put it in honey, and whenever he was about to do anything, he would stoop over the vessel and tell all that he was doing, saying that he was not breaking faith nor perjuring himself, but taking counsel with the head of Archonides.

9. Timesias of Clazomenae governed the Clazomenians well; for he was one of the good men. But envy, which is wont to prevail against such men, prevailed against Timesias too. At first he cared little for being envied, but the following thing, they say, drove him from his country. He was passing by a school; and the boys, having been let out by their teacher, were playing. A dispute arose between two boys over a line, and one of them swore: "So may I dash out the brains of Timesias!" Hearing this, and supposing that envy of him was unrestrained and that he was terribly hated by his citizens, since even the boys hated him — let alone the men — he willingly departed from his country.

10. The Aeginetans once were the most powerful among the Greeks, having obtained a certain abundance of wealth and good fortune; for they had a naval force and were very great. In the Persian wars too they proved brave, and for this were judged worthy of the prizes of valour. And they first struck coinage, the coin called after them the Aeginetan.
11. The Romans, beneath the Palatine hill, set up a temple and an altar to Fever.

12. An adulterer caught in Gortyn was brought before the magistrates; then, convicted, he was crowned with wool. This crowning signified that he was unmanly and womanish and lustful after women. And he was sold publicly and was most dishonoured and had no share in public affairs.

13. There came from the Hellespont to the Attic courtesan Gnathaena a man as a lover, drawn by her fame. So over the wine he talked much, and seemed tiresome. Gnathaena, taking him up, said to him: "So you say you have come from the Hellespont?" When he agreed, she said: "And how is it you do not know the first of the cities there?" When he said, "And which is this?" she answered, "Sigeum." And by means of the name she fittingly silenced him.

14. The most beautiful and lovable of men, they say, were, among the Greeks Alcibiades, and among the Romans Scipio. They say too that Demetrius Poliorcetes laid claim to beauty. And Alexander son of Philip, they say, was beautiful without effort; for his hair was swept back and was golden, and there shone forth from his appearance, they say, something awe-inspiring in Alexander.

15. They say that Heracles rested his labours in the contests with play. The son of Zeus and Alcmene was very fond of playing with children. This Euripides too hints at to us, making this same god say: "I play; for I ever love changes from toil." He says this while holding a child. And Socrates was once caught by Alcibiades playing with Lamprocles, who was still an infant. And Agesilaus, bestriding a reed, rode it with his son, who was a boy, and to the one who laughed he said: "For now be silent, but when you become a father yourself, then you will tell of it." And Archytas of Tarentum too, a statesman and a philosopher, having many household slaves, took great delight in playing with their children, the home-bred slaves; and most of all he liked to delight in them at his banquets.

16. Alexander son of Philip is said to have been most jealously disposed toward his companions, and to have envied them all, though not for the same reasons. For he was vexed with Perdiccas because he was warlike, with Lysimachus because he seemed a good general, with Seleucus because he was brave; Antigonus's ambition pained him, with Antipater he was vexed for his capacity to command, Ptolemy's cleverness he viewed with suspicion, Tarrias's unruliness he feared, and Pithon's revolutionary spirit.

17. Demetrius, though he ruled over so many nations, used to go to Lamia the courtesan with his arms and wearing his diadem. It was shameful enough for him even to send for the woman to his house; but he would go to her openly. For my part, I would prefer Theodorus the flute-player to Demetrius, since when Lamia sent for Theodorus, he disdained the summons.

18. Phaon, who was the fairest of men, Aphrodite hid among the lettuces. Another tale is that he was a ferryman and had this occupation. Aphrodite once came, wishing to cross over, and he received her gladly, not knowing who she was, and with much care brought her wherever she wished. In return the goddess gave him an alabaster jar, and it held an ointment, with which Phaon, anointing himself, became the fairest of men; and the women of Mytilene fell in love with him. At the last, however, he was slain, caught in adultery.
19. The poetess Sappho, daughter of Scamandronymus — her even Plato son of Ariston records as wise. I learn that there was also another Sappho in Lesbos, a courtesan, not a poetess.

20. Hesiod says that the nightingale alone of birds has no share in sleep and is wakeful throughout; but that the swallow does not keep wholly wakeful even she, but has lost half her sleep. They pay this penalty for the suffering committed in Thrace, that lawless dinner.

21. The mothers of the Lacedaemonians, all who learned that their sons lay slain in battle, came and inspected their wounds, both those in front and those behind. And if the wounds in front were more, they, exulting and looking at once proud and stern, carried their sons off to the ancestral tombs; but if it was otherwise with the wounds, then, ashamed and lamenting and eager to escape notice as much as possible, they went away, leaving the dead to be buried in the common grave, or carried them secretly to the family tombs.

22. They say that Milo of Croton, who was proud because of his bodily strength, met Titormus the cowherd. Seeing, then, that Titormus was great of body to look upon, he wished to make trial of his strength. But Titormus said that he had no great strength, and going down to the Evenus and stripping off his cloak, he took a very large stone, and first drew it toward himself, then pushed it away, and did this twice and three times, and after that raised it as far as his knees, and finally lifting it onto his shoulders carried it some eight fathoms and threw it; but Milo of Croton could barely move the stone. Then Titormus went to the herd, and standing in the midst he took the largest bull, which was wild, by the foot; and the bull was eager to escape, but could not. And as another passed by, he seized it likewise by the foot with his other hand and held it. Milo, seeing this, stretched his hands to heaven and said: "O Zeus, have you not begotten for us a second Heracles in this man?" From this, they say, the proverb arose: "This is another Heracles."

23. Of men I hear that the Celts are the fondest of danger. At any rate they make the subjects of their songs the men who have died nobly in war. They fight crowned with garlands, and they raise trophies too, at once taking pride in their deeds and leaving behind memorials of their valour in the Greek manner. So shameful do they think it to flee, that they will not run away even from their houses when these are sliding and collapsing, nor even when they are on fire and they are surrounded by the flames. Many even stand fast against the flooding sea. There are some too who, taking up their arms, fall upon the waves and receive their onset, brandishing their naked swords and spears, as though they could either frighten or wound them.

24. They say that Smindyrides the Sybarite ran aground in such luxury that he came to Sicyon as a suitor of Agariste the daughter of Cleisthenes, and brought with him a thousand cooks, as many fowlers, and a thousand fishermen.

25. Odysseus profited from Alcinous, and Achilles from Chiron, and Patroclus from Achilles, and Agamemnon from Nestor, and Telemachus from Menelaus, and Hector from Polydamas, in the matters in which he gave heed to him, and the Trojans from Antenor. And the Pythagoreans, the disciples of Pythagoras, profited, and the Democriteans, having associated with Democritus, enjoyed many benefits. And if the Athenians had given heed to Socrates, they would all have become happy. Hiero son of Deinomenes profited from Simonides of Ceos, and Polycrates from Anacreon, and Proxenus from Xenophon, and Antigonus from Zeno. And that I may make mention of those who belong to me no less than the Greeks belong — for this concerns me too, since I am a Roman — Lucullus profited something from Antiochus of Ascalon, and Maecenas from Areius, and Cicero from Apollonius, and Augustus from Athenodorus. And Plato, though wiser than I, says that even Zeus had a counsellor; who, and how, let us learn from him.

26. The hardest drinkers, they say, have been Xenagoras of Rhodes, whom they called "the Amphora," and Heracleides the boxer, and Proteas the son of Lanice, the foster-brother of King Alexander. And Alexander himself is said to have drunk the most of men.

27. They say that Heracles behaved most humanely toward his own enemies; for he was the first from the beginning of time to give back the dead under truce to be buried, whereas the men of that time were wont to neglect the slain and leave them to be a meal for dogs.

28. The Leocorion at Athens was the name of the precinct of the daughters of Leos — Praxithea and Theope and Euboule. The story is that these were put to death for the city of the Athenians, Leos having given them up at the bidding of the Delphic oracle. For it said that the city could not otherwise be saved, unless they were sacrificed.

29. Plato son of Ariston, seeing the people of Acragas both building lavishly and likewise dining, said that the Acragantines build as though they would live forever, but dine as though they would die tomorrow. Timaeus says that they used silver oil-flasks and strigils and had whole couches of ivory.

30. The Tarentines had the custom of drinking from early morning and being drunk about the time the marketplace is full. And the Cyrenaeans ran aground in such luxury that they invited Plato to be their lawgiver. But he refused, they say, because of their inveterate indolence. Eupolis too agrees, in the Maricas, that the cheapest of them had signet-rings worth ten minae. And the engravers of the rings were also admired.

31. Come, let me recite to you the names of the Greek wines that were sought after in old times. One they called Pramnian, and this was sacred to Demeter. And there was Chian wine from the island, and another Thasian, and Lesbian. Besides these there was one called "Sweet," fitting its name in taste, and another Cretan. And in Syracuse there was Pollian; it was named after a certain local king. They drank Coan wine too, and so called it; and Rhodian, naming it in the same way. And what of this? Was it not a proof of luxury among the Greeks? For they mixed wine with myrrh and so drank it, and greatly delighted in such a mixture; and the wine was called "Myrrhine." Philippides the comic poet mentions it.

32. Pythagoras of Samos wore white clothing, and a golden crown, and trousers. Empedocles of Acragas used purple and bronze sandals. And the report goes that Hippias and Gorgias went about in purple robes.

33. Cineas, the physician of Pyrrhus, they say, wrote secretly to the council of the Romans, and asked for money, and promised to kill Pyrrhus by poisons. But they did not accept the offer; for the Romans know how to be good through virtue, not to overcome their enemies through craft and villainy and treachery. They even revealed to Pyrrhus himself the design of Cineas.

34. Many loves of the ancients have been handed down to our memory, and these not least. Pausanias loved his own wife, and Apelles the concubine of Alexander, whose name was Pancaste, and who was Larissaean by birth. With her, they say, Alexander first consorted.

35. There were two Perianders, the one a wise man, the other a tyrant. And three Miltiadeses: the one who founded the Chersonese, and the son of Cypselus, and the son of Cimon. Four Sibyls: the Erythraean, the Samian, the Egyptian, the Sardian. Some say there were six others, so that there were ten in all, of whom were the Cumaean and the Jewish. Three Bacides: the one of Eleon, the one of Athens, the one of Arcadia.

36. The ancients seem not to agree with one another about the number of Niobe's children. Homer says six sons and as many daughters; Lasus says twice seven; Hesiod nineteen — unless indeed the verses are not Hesiod's, but, as many other things, are falsely ascribed to him. Alcman says ten; Mimnermus twenty; and Pindar as many.

37. Alexander, when he was pursuing Bessus, finding himself in want of food, took to eating the camels and other beasts of burden, both he and those with him. And when their firewood failed them, they ate the meat raw. The silphium, which was plentiful, helped them, so as to digest the flesh. And in Bactria the soldiers found the villages, learning that they were inhabited by the smoke, and clearing the snow away from the doors.

38. The horses of the Sacae, if one throws his master, stand still for him to mount again. If anyone wishes to marry a maiden, he fights in single combat with the girl. And if she wins, she leads him captive and has power and rule over him; but if she is beaten, she is ruled. They fight in single combat to victory, not to death. The Sacae, when they mourn, hide themselves in certain caverned and shady houses.

39. Perdiccas the Macedonian, who campaigned with Alexander, was so daring that he once went alone into a cave where a lioness had her lair; and the lioness he did not find, but he came out carrying her cubs, and for this Perdiccas was thought to be admired. It is believed, not only among the Greeks but also among the barbarians, that the lioness is the boldest and hardest to fight of beasts. They say, at any rate, that Semiramis the Assyrian was not proud if ever she took a lion or killed a leopard or any such thing, but only if she got the better of a lioness.

40. Among the other supplies that followed Xerxes, full of extravagance and ostentation, there followed also water from the Choaspes. And when in some desert place he was thirsty, his attendants not yet having come, it was proclaimed to the army that, if anyone had water from the Choaspes, he should give the king to drink. And someone was found who had a little, and that putrid. So Xerxes drank it, and considered the giver his benefactor, because he would have perished of thirst, had not that man been found.

41. Protogenes the painter, they say, completed his Ialysus, painting it over seven years. When Apelles saw it, at first he stood speechless, astounded at the marvellous sight, then said: "Great is the labour and great the craftsman; yet his handiwork lacks the grace which, if the man should attain it, his labour would touch heaven itself."

42. Cyrus, the son of Mandane, was reared, they say, by a dog; Telephus, the son of Auge and Heracles, by a hind; Pelias, the son of Poseidon and Tyro, by a horse, and so too the son of Alope. Alexander son of Priam, they say, was reared by a bear, and Aegisthus, the son of Thyestes and Pelopia, by a goat.

43. I hear that Darius the son of Hystaspes was a quiver-bearer of Cyrus. And the last Darius, who was defeated by Alexander, was a slave. Archelaus the king of the Macedonians was the son of a slave-woman, Simiche. Menelaus the grandfather of Philip was reckoned among the bastards. His son Amyntas was believed to be the servant and slave of Aeropus. Perseus, whom Paulus the Roman overthrew, was Argive by birth, the son of some obscure man. Eumenes is believed to have been the son of a poor father and a grave-flute-player. Antigonus son of Philip, who had but one eye and was therefore called Cyclops, was a man who worked with his own hands. Polysperchon was a brigand. Themistocles, who defeated the barbarians at sea and alone understood the voices of the gods in the oracles, was the son of a Thracian woman, and his mother was called Abrotonon. Phocion, surnamed the Good, was the son of a man who made pestles, and Demetrius of Phalerum, they say, was a home-bred slave from the house of Timotheus and Conon. As for Hyperbolus and Cleophon and Demades, although they became leaders of the Athenian people, no one could easily say who their fathers were. Callicratidas and Gylippus and Lysander in Lacedaemon were called Mothakes. This was the name for the slaves of the wealthy, whom their fathers sent out with their sons to share their training in the gymnasia. And Lycurgus, who allowed this, granted a share in the Laconian citizenship to those who kept to the rearing of children. And Epaminondas was the son of an obscure father. And Cleon the tyrant of the Sicyonians was a pirate who threw men into the sea.

44. The quarries in Sicily were near Epipolae, a stade in length and two plethra in breadth. And there were men who had spent so much time in them that they had even married there and begotten children. And some of those children, never having seen a city, when they came to Syracuse and saw horses yoked and oxen being driven, fled crying out; so astonished were they. The fairest of the caverns there was named after Philoxenus the poet, in which, they say, he composed, while spending time there, the fairest of his songs, the Cyclops, setting at nothing the vengeance and condemnation of Dionysius, but making music, Philoxenus, in the very midst of his misfortune.

45. The Phrygian tales sing these things too. That while Midas the Phrygian was still an infant sleeping, ants crept into his mouth, and most laboriously and industriously carried in grains of wheat. And that bees made a honeycomb in the mouth of Plato. And to Pindar, exposed from his father's house, bees became nurses, providing honey in place of milk.

46. Dionysius the son of Hermocrates, they say, was crossing a river; a horse was carrying him. And the horse slipped into the mire, and he leaped off and caught hold of the bank and went away, leaving the horse as though it were no longer his. But the horse followed and, with a whinny, turned him back. And he caught hold of its mane and was about to mount, when a swarm of bees fell upon his hand. The Galeotae, then, when Dionysius asked them about this, said that these things signified monarchy.

47. Dionysius drove Dion out of Sicily, but kept his wife Arete and his son by him under guard. Later he gave the wife, against her will, in marriage to Timocrates, his bodyguard, who was of all men his greatest attendant; he was a Syracusan by birth. But Dion, when he took over Syracuse, Dionysius having fled to the Locrians, then Aristomache the sister of Dion greeted him. And Arete followed, veiling herself for shame and not daring to greet him as her husband, since, forced, she had not kept faith with the bed she shared with him. When Aristomache had pleaded for her, recounting the compulsion laid on her by Dionysius, Dion took back his wife and child and sent them to his house.

48. The Indians, having translated the verses of Homer into their own native tongue, sing them — not they alone, but also the kings of the Persians, if one is to believe at all those who relate these things.

49. Phocion the son of Phocus, who had often been general, was condemned to death, and was in prison and about to drink the hemlock.
