When the executioner held out the cup, his kinsmen asked if he had anything to say to his son. And he said: "I charge him to bear the Athenians no grudge for this loving-cup which I now drink." Whoever does not praise and greatly admire this man seems to me to have no great thought in him.

50. The Lacedaemonians had no experience of music; for their care was for gymnastics and arms. But if ever they needed help from the Muses, whether falling sick or going mad or suffering some other such thing publicly, they would send for foreign men, like physicians or purifiers, according to the Pythian oracle. They sent, indeed, for Terpander and Thales and Tyrtaeus and Nymphaeus of Cydonia and Alcman. And Thucydides too admits that they were not zealous for culture, where he speaks of Brasidas. For he says that he was not even incapable of speaking, for a Lacedaemonian.

51. Menecrates the physician advanced to such a pitch of conceit that he called himself Zeus. He once sent to Philip the king of the Macedonians a letter of this kind: "Menecrates Zeus to Philip, greeting." And Philip wrote back: "Philip to Menecrates, health. I advise you to take yourself off to the regions about Anticyra." He hinted by this that the man was mad. Philip once gave a magnificent feast, and indeed invited this man to the banquet, and ordered a separate couch to be prepared for him, and when he had reclined, set before him a censer and burned incense to him; while the rest feasted, and the dinner was magnificent. So Menecrates at first held out, and rejoiced in the honour; but when little by little hunger came over him, and he was shown to be a man, and a foolish one at that, he rose up and went off, and said he had been insulted — Philip having very fittingly uncovered his folly.

52. Isocrates the orator used to say of the city of the Athenians that it was like the courtesans. For those who are captivated by their beauty wish to be with them, yet no one is so cheaply foolish as to endure to live with one of them. And so the city of the Athenians is most pleasant to visit, and in this surpasses all the cities in Greece; but to dwell in is no longer safe. He hinted by this at the informers who haunted it and the plots of the demagogues.

53. It has not escaped me that the beginnings of the greatest wars seem somehow to have been contemptible. For they say that the Persian war took its beginning from the quarrel of Maeandrius of Samos with the Athenians, and the Peloponnesian from the decree against the Megarians, and the one called Sacred from the exaction of fines by the Amphictyons, and the war at Chaeronea from the Athenians' contention with Philip and their refusal to come to terms.

54. Aristotle, wishing to soothe Alexander when he was angry and to stop him from being harsh with many, wrote thus to him: "Wrath and anger arise not against inferiors, but against superiors; and to you no one is equal." Aristotle, by giving Alexander the needful counsel, became a benefactor to many, by which means he restored his native city, which had been razed by Philip.

55. Those who are killed by elephants, whether in the hunts or in the battles, the Libyans bury with distinction, and sing certain hymns. The burden of the hymns is this: it says that they were brave men who fought against so great a beast; for they say that a glorious death is a burial-honour for the one buried.

56. Diogenes of Sinope said many things in disparagement of the ignorance and lack of culture of the Megarians, and said he would rather be a Megarian man's ram than his son. He hinted that the Megarians take thought for their flocks, but not for their children.

57. When Alexander son of Philip was leading his force against Thebes, the gods sent them signs and portents, foreshadowing the fortunes that all but immediately awaited them; but they, thinking that Alexander had died among the Illyrians, cast many blasphemies against him. For the lake at Onchestus gave forth a fearful and continuous sound, and was like the bellowing of a bull; and the spring called Dirce, flowing by the Ismenium and the very walls, which all the time before had flowed with clear and sweet water, suddenly and beyond expectation was filled with blood. The Thebans believed that the divine power was threatening the Macedonians. And in the temple of Demeter in the city a spider wove its web over the face of the statue. And the statue of Athena called Alalcomeneis was burned of itself, no fire being applied; and many other things.

58. Dioxippus the Olympic victor, the athlete, the Athenian, was riding into Athens according to the custom of athletes. So the crowds streamed together, and people, hanging from this place and that, gazed at him; and among them a woman of outstanding beauty met the spectacle. Dioxippus, seeing her, was at once overcome by her beauty, and kept gazing at the woman and turning round and changing his face to many colours. From this it became plain to many that he had not looked at the woman idly. Above all Diogenes of Sinope marked his condition, and said to those near him: "See your great athlete thrown by a slip of a girl."
59. Pythagoras used to say that these two finest things were given to men by the gods: to speak the truth and to do good; and he added that each of them resembled the works of the gods.

60. There was once a meeting between Dionysius the Second and Philip the son of Amyntas. Many other topics, as was natural, came up; and among them Philip asked Dionysius how it was that, having received so great a rule from his father, he then did not preserve it. And he answered, not out of tune: "My father left me everything else, but the fortune by which he gained and kept these things, that he left me no longer."

61. Dionysius sailed against Thurii, and brought against them three hundred ships filled with soldiers; but a north wind blowing against him shattered the vessels and destroyed his naval force. From this the Thurians sacrificed to the North Wind, and decreed that the wind should be a citizen, and allotted him a house and a portion of land, and every year performed rites to him. So not only did the Athenians consider him their kinsman by marriage, but the Thurians too inscribed him as their benefactor. And Pausanias says that the Megalopolitans did so too.

62. This too is a Persian law. If anyone is about to advise the king on some secret and disputed matter, he stands upon a golden brick. And if he seems to advise what is needful, he takes the brick and goes away with it as a reward for his counsel; but he is nonetheless flogged, because he has contradicted the king. To a free man, in my judgment, the insult is no fit counterweight to the reward.

63. A certain Archedice fell in love with the courtesan in Naucratis. But she was haughty and terribly tiresome and demanded heavy fees, and having taken them she would consort for a little while with the giver, then turn away. So the young man, in love with her, and unable to win her because he was not very rich, consorted with her in a dream, and at once ceased from his desire.

64. Alexander, the son of Philip and Olympias, having ended his life in Babylon, lay a corpse — he who said he was the son of Zeus. And while those about him quarrelled over the kingdom, he was without a share in burial, which even the very poor obtain, since the common nature of things demands that one no longer living be hidden away. But he was left uncared-for for thirty days, until Aristander of Telmessus, possessed by a god or held by some other chance, came into the midst of the Macedonians and said to them that Alexander had been the most fortunate of all the kings from the beginning of time, both living and dead; for the gods told him that the land that received the body, in which his soul had formerly dwelt, would be wholly blessed and unravaged through all time. Hearing this, they were filled with great rivalry, each desiring to carry off this precious freight to his own kingdom, that he might have a treasure and a pledge of secure and unshaken rule. But Ptolemy, if one is to believe it, stole the body away, and with haste carried it to the city of Alexander in Egypt. And the other Macedonians kept quiet, but Perdiccas set about pursuing him. It was not so much that he cared for the honour of Alexander and the rites due to the dead, as that the words spoken beforehand by Aristander inflamed and kindled him. When he overtook Ptolemy, a most fierce battle arose over the corpse, sister in a way to that over the phantom at Troy, which Homer sings, telling how Apollo cast a phantom of Aeneas into the midst of the heroes. But Ptolemy checked the onset of Perdiccas; for making a phantom like Alexander, he adorned it with royal dress and enviable burial-trappings. Then setting this up upon one of the Persian wagons, he furnished the bier upon it magnificently with silver and gold and ivory; and the real body of Alexander he sent forward plainly and as it chanced, by hidden and untrodden roads. And Perdiccas, overtaking the phantom of the corpse and the decked-out wagon, was checked in his course, thinking he had the prize; but too late he learned that he had been deceived, when he could not pursue."

1. This is an Arcadian tale about Atalanta the daughter of Iasion. Her father, when she was born, exposed her; for he said that he had need not of daughters but of sons. But the man who took her to expose her did not kill her, and going to Mount Parthenium he laid her near a spring; and there was a hollow rock there, and above it lay a thick-covered thicket. Death had been decreed for the infant, but she was not betrayed by fortune; for a little later a bear, robbed of her own cubs by hunters, came, her teats swollen and heavy with milk. Then, by some divine guidance, taking pleasure in the infant, she suckled it, and at once the beast was relieved of its pain and gave nourishment to the infant. And so, again pouring out her milk and giving suck, since she had not remained a mother to her own, she became nurse to one who was nothing to her. The hunters who from the first had plotted against the beast over her offspring kept watch on her, and having observed each thing that was done, when the bear had gone off as usual to hunt and graze, they carried off Atalanta — though she was not yet so called, for they themselves gave her the name. And she was reared by them on a mountain diet. Little by little her body grew with her age; and she loved virginity and shunned the company of men and longed for solitude, taking the highest of the Arcadian mountains, where there was a well-watered glen and great oaks, and also pines and the deep shade they cast. For what harm does it do us to hear of Atalanta's cave too, as of Calypso's in Homer? In the hollow ravine there was a cave, one and very deep, and in front it was guarded by a deep precipice. Ivy crept around it, and the ivy twined with soft trees and crept up through them. Crocuses too grew about the place in the soft and deep grass. And with them sprang up the hyacinth and many another colour of flowers, able not only to furnish a feast for the eyes, but the scents from them filled the air all around; and one could keep festival both in other ways and feast upon the fragrance. There were many laurels too, the sweet foliage of a plant ever in its bloom to look upon; and vines, flourishing with very plentiful clusters before the cave, displayed the industry of Atalanta. And waters perpetual and ever-flowing, clear to see and cold, as far as one could judge by touch and tell by drinking, flowed in abundance and without stint; and these same waters were also fit for the watering of the trees aforesaid, flowing continually and helping toward their life. So the place was full of graces, and showed at once a most venerable and a chaste maiden's chamber. Atalanta's bedding was the hides of the beasts she had hunted, her food their flesh, her drink the water. She wore a plain dress, of a kind not out of tune with Artemis; for she said that she emulated the goddess both in this and in wishing to be a virgin throughout. She was very swift of foot, and neither beast nor man plotting against her could escape her; and when she wished to flee, no one could overtake her. And not only those who saw her loved her, but already from report men loved her too. Come, let me describe her appearance too, if it does no harm; and it does none, since from this too may be gained both experience and art of words. In height, while still a child, she was beyond grown women; and she was beautiful, as no other of the maidens then in the Peloponnese. Her look was masculine and fierce, this both from her wild rearing and now too from her exercises in the mountains. She had nothing girlish or delicate; for she did not come forth from a bridal chamber, nor was she of those reared under mothers and nurses. Nor did she have the over-plump body either, and that quite naturally, since in the hunts and at the very exercises she worked her whole body hard. Her hair was golden, in no way by womanly fussiness and dyes and cosmetics, but the colour was the work of nature. Her face was reddened too by the suns, and looked like a flush outright. And what flower could be so beautiful as the face of a maiden trained to modesty? She had two startling things: matchless beauty, and with it the power to frighten too. No idle man would have loved her at the sight, nor would he even have dared to look her in the face at first; so great was the radiance that shone, with her beauty, on those who saw her. She was hard to meet, both in other ways and for her rarity. For one could not easily see her; but unexpectedly and unforeseen she would appear, chasing a beast or defending herself against someone, darting like a star, then she would hide herself, running through a thicket or a copse or some other dense growth in the mountain. Once, at midnight, those who dwelt near her — bold lovers and most tiresome revellers — came in revel, two of the Centaurs, Hylaeus and Rhoecus. Their revel was no flute-girls nor indeed the doings of the young men of the city, but pine-torches, and lighting and kindling these, by the first appearance of the fire they would have startled even a whole people, let alone a single maiden. Breaking off fresh-cut boughs of pines, then plaiting them together, they made themselves crowns. Continually and frequently clashing their weapons through the mountains, setting fire to the trees as well, they pressed on toward the girl, evil suitors, with insolence and frenzy paying beforehand the wedding-gifts of their marriage. But the plot did not escape her; seeing the fire from the cave and recognizing who these revellers were, in no way dismayed nor cowering at the sight, she bent her bow, let fly her arrow, and hit the first very opportunely. And he lay there, while the second came on, no longer in revel-fashion but now in war-fashion, wishing to defend his comrade and to glut his own onset. But to him too the girl's other arrow came as avenger. So much, then, for Atalanta the daughter of Iasion.

2. There was a man of Mytilene, Macareus by name, a priest of Dionysus, who, so far as appearance went, was gentle and fair, but most impious of men above all. A stranger came to him and gave him a great quantity of gold for safekeeping; and Macareus, digging up the ground in the innermost part of the temple, buried the gold. In time the stranger came and demanded the gold back. He, leading him inside as though to give it back, cut his throat, dug up the gold, and put the stranger in its place; and he thought that, as he had escaped men's notice, so he would escape the god's too. But this turned out not so; how could it? When a little time had passed, the god's triennial festival came, and he sacrificed magnificently. And while he was occupied with the Bacchic rites, his children, two in number, were left behind inside the house, and imitating their father's sacred rite they came to the ancestral altar while the offerings were still burning; and the younger offered his neck, and the elder, finding a sacrificial knife that had been left lying, killed his brother like a victim. Those in the house, seeing it, cried out. The mother, hearing the cry, rushed out, and seeing the one dead and the other still holding the bloody knife, snatched up a half-burnt billet from the altar and with it killed the boy. News came to Macareus, and leaving the rite, just as he was, with wrath and fury he rushed into the house, and with the thyrsus he was holding killed his own wife. So his deeds became known to all, and Macareus, arrested and tortured, confessed all that he had done in the temple; and amid the very tortures he gave up his life. And the man unlawfully slain came to public honour, and was buried at the god's command. So Macareus paid no slight penalty — to use the poet's phrase — with his own head and his wife's and, moreover, his children's too.

3. Xerxes the son of Darius, digging up the tomb of the ancient Belus, found a glass coffin, where the corpse lay in oil. The coffin was not full, but fell short of the rim by about a hand's breadth. Beside the coffin lay a short pillar, on which was written: "For him who opens the tomb and does not fill up the coffin, it shall not be better." Reading this, Xerxes was afraid, and ordered oil to be poured in as quickly as possible; yet it was not filled. He ordered more to be poured in. But it took no increase, until he gave up, spending in vain what he poured. Shutting up the tomb, he went away in distress. And the pillar did not lie in what it had foretold; for having gathered seven hundred thousand men against the Greeks, he fared ill, then returning home died the most shameful of deaths, slain by night in his bed by his son.

4. King Archelaus prepared a costly feast for his companions. As the drinking went on, Euripides, having drunk rather strong wine, was somehow drawn little by little into intoxication; then, embracing Agathon the tragic poet, who was reclining beside him, he kissed him, though he was about forty years old. When Archelaus asked whether he still seemed to him to be a beloved, he answered: "Yes, by Zeus; for not only the spring of the beautiful is fairest, but the autumn too."

5. They say that Laius was the first to fall in love with noble youths, having carried off Chrysippus the son of Pelops. And from this it seemed to the Thebans one of the fine things to love youths in their bloom.

6. In Heraea in Arcadia, I hear, there grow vines from which comes a wine that turns men's reason aside and makes the Arcadians frenzied, but makes the women fruitful. In Thasos, they say, two kinds of wine are produced; and the one, when drunk, brings on a very deep and therefore pleasant sleep, but the other is an enemy to life and produces wakefulness and gives distress. And in Achaea, near Ceryneia, a wine is produced that helps the women who wish to miscarry.

7. When Alexander took the city of the Thebans, he sold all the free men except the priests. He exempted from sale also his father's guest-friends — for Philip had been a hostage among them while still a boy — and he released their kinsmen too. He honoured the descendants of Pindar, and allowed his house alone to stand. He killed about six thousand of the Thebans, and thirty thousand were taken captive.
8. They say that Lysander the Lacedaemonian, while spending time in Ionia, cast aside the ordinances of Lycurgus, since they were toilsome, and dissolved his life in luxury.
9. Lamia the Attic courtesan said: "The lions from Greece have become foxes in Ephesus."

10. On one day Dionysius married two wives, Doris the Locrian and Aristomache the daughter of Hipparinus, the sister of Dion; and he slept with each in turn. And the one followed him when he campaigned, the other received him on his return.

11. An account has come to me saying that Isocrates the orator was the cause to the Persians of the enslavement by which the Macedonians enslaved them. For when the fame of the panegyric speech which Isocrates delivered among the Greeks came to Macedonia, it first roused Philip against Asia; and when he died, it prepared Alexander his son, the heir of his father's possessions, to take up the impulse of Philip.

12. Meton the astronomer, when the Athenians were about to sail against Sicily, was himself already one of the levy. But knowing clearly the fortunes that were to come, he tried to avoid the voyage, fearing it and eager to free himself from the expedition. When he could accomplish nothing, he feigned madness; and he did many other things, wishing to confirm the belief in his sickness, and among them he burned down his own dwelling, which was near the Stoa Poikile. From this the magistrates released him. And it seems to me that Meton feigned madness better than Odysseus of Ithaca; for Palamedes detected that man, but no one of the Athenians detected this one.
13. They say that Ptolemy the son of Lagus took great delight in enriching his friends. And he used to say that it was better to make others rich than to be rich oneself.

14. The verses of Homer the ancients formerly sang divided into parts. For instance, they spoke of "The Battle at the Ships" and a certain "Doloneia" and "The Aristeia of Agamemnon" and "The Catalogue of Ships" and "The Patrocleia" and "The Ransom" and "The Games over Patroclus" and "The Breaking of the Oaths." These for the Iliad. And for the other: "The Events in Pylos" and "The Events in Lacedaemon" and "Calypso's Cave" and "The Affair of the Raft" and "The Tales told to Alcinous" and "The Cyclops" and "The Descent to the Dead" and "The Affairs of Circe" and "The Washing of the Feet" and "The Slaying of the Suitors" and "The Events in the Country" and "The Events at Laertes'." Late, Lycurgus the Lacedaemonian was the first to bring the poetry of Homer in a body to Greece; and he brought this freight from Ionia, when he was abroad. Later Pisistratus gathered it together and produced the Iliad and the Odyssey.

15. The comic poets say that a certain Polydorus was the dullest of mind, and another one named Coecylion, who counted the waves out of excessive folly. There is a story too that Sannyrion was such a man, who looked for a ladder in an oil-flask. And Coroebus and Melitides too they call those fools.

16. The Apolloniatae inhabit a city near Epidamnus on the Ionian gulf. And in the places near it there is asphalt that is dug up, and pitch springing from the earth in the same way as do most of the springs of water. Not far off the immortal fire too is shown. The burning place is small and does not extend far and has no great circuit, and smells of sulphur and alum. And about it are flourishing trees and green grass; and the fire blazing nearby does no harm either to the growth of the plants or to the flourishing grass. The fire burns both by night and by day, and never ceased, as the Apolloniatae say, until the war with the Illyrians befell them. The Apolloniatae practised the expulsion of foreigners according to the Lacedaemonian law, but the Epidamnians allowed anyone who wished to visit and settle among them.

17. "Phrynichus cowers like a cock" — a proverb said of those who suffer some ill. For when Phrynichus the tragedian was performing The Capture of Miletus, the Athenians, bursting into tears, expelled him as he cowered and crouched in fear.
18. Dionysius the tyrant of Sicily embraced and praised tragedy, and indeed worked at composing tragic dramas, but was disposed unfavourably toward comedy, because he was not fond of laughter.

19. Cleomenes said, in the Laconian manner after the local fashion, that Homer was the poet of the Lacedaemonians, since he tells how one must make war; but Hesiod the poet of the Helots, since he tells how one must farm.

20. A man of Megalopolis from Arcadia, Cercidas by name, as he was dying said to his kinsmen, who were downcast, that he was leaving life gladly; for he had hope of consorting, among the wise, with Pythagoras, among the historians with Hecataeus, among the musicians with Olympus, among the poets with Homer. And with these words, the story goes, his soul left him.
21. In Celaenae, if anyone plays upon the flute, before the skin of the Phrygian, the Phrygian mode, the skin moves; but if the mode is for Apollo, it stays still and seems deaf.

22. Ptolemy Philopator, having built a temple to Homer, set him fairly seated and beautiful, and set in a circle around the statue all the cities that lay claim to Homer. And Galaton the painter painted Homer himself vomiting, and the other poets drawing up what he had vomited.

23. Lycurgus the Lacedaemonian, the son of Eunomus, wishing to make the Lacedaemonians just, drew for this no fine wages. For it befell him to have his eye knocked out by Alcander, as some say, struck with a stone out of a plot, or, as another story goes about, suffering the injury from a staff. The saying is applied to those who wished for one thing but obtained another. And Ephorus says that he died in exile, having held out against hunger.

24. Lycurgus the orator proposed that women should not drive in carriages at the mysteries, or that a penalty be imposed on her who did this, which he thought sufficient when he fixed it. The first to disobey the decree was his own wife, and she paid the penalty, being condemned. And Pericles proposed that no one should be an Athenian who was not born of two citizens. Then, having lost his legitimate sons, he was left with the bastard Pericles. It is plain that Pericles too wished for one thing but obtained another. And Cleisthenes the Athenian, who first proposed that men should be ostracized, was himself the first to incur the sentence. Zaleucus the lawgiver of the Locrians ordered that an adulterer caught should have his eyes put out. So things he had not even expected the divine power brought upon him contrary to his judgment and his hope; for his own son, caught in adultery, was then about to suffer what the ancestral law required. There, that what had once been ratified might not be undone, the proposer himself submitted to give his own eye in exchange for one of his son's eyes, that the young man might not be wholly blinded.
25. Pindar the poet, competing in Thebes and falling among ignorant hearers, was defeated by Corinna five times. Exposing their want of culture, Pindar called Corinna a sow.

26. Diogenes of Sinope was solitary and cast off alone, and no one received him because of his poverty, nor did anyone entertain him, shunning the man because of the censorious nature of his character and because he was hard to please at what was done and said. So Diogenes was downcast and ate the tips of leaves; for these he had at hand. And a mouse came and made use of the crumbs that fell from his bread. So Diogenes carefully observed what was happening, and smiling and coming to himself, more cheerful and serene, he said: "This mouse has no need of the luxury of the Athenians, but you, Diogenes, are vexed because you do not dine with the Athenians." And he procured himself a timely cheerfulness.

27. The body of Socrates is believed to have been orderly and master of self-restraint, and in this way. The Athenians were sick in a general plague, and some died, others were near death; but Socrates alone did not fall sick at all. The man, then, who dwelt in such a body — what kind of soul do we think he had?

28. Diogenes, when he left his country, was followed by one of his servants named Manes, who, not bearing his way of life with him, ran away. When some urged him to seek the man out, he said: "Is it not shameful that Manes has no need of Diogenes, but Diogenes of Manes?" This servant, wandering to Delphi, was torn apart by dogs, paying the penalty for his master's name in return for his running away.
29. Plato used to say that the hopes of waking men are dreams.

30. Olympias, the mother of Alexander, learning that her son remained a long time unburied, groaning heavily and lamenting very shrilly, said: "O my child, you who wished to share in heaven and were eager for this, now you cannot even share in what is common and equal to all men — earth and burial." So she pitied her own fortunes and rebuked the conceit of her son.

31. Xenocrates of Chalcedon, the companion of Plato, was both compassionate in other ways and not only a lover of mankind but also pitied many of the irrational animals. So once, as he was sitting in the open air, a sparrow, hotly pursued by a hawk, flew into his bosom. He gladly received the bird, and kept it hidden until the pursuer had gone away. When he had freed it from fear, opening his bosom he let the bird go, saying that he had not betrayed a suppliant.

32. Xenophon says that Socrates came to converse with Theodote the courtesan, who was a most beautiful woman. And he came to converse with Callisto too, who said: "I, son of Sophroniscus, am stronger than you; for you cannot draw away any of mine, but I, if I wish, can draw away all of yours." And he said: "Yes, and with good reason; for you lead them down the easy path, but I force them to come to virtue; and the way up is steep and unfamiliar to most."

33. They say that the Egyptian tales tell of Rhodopis, a most beautiful courtesan. Once, as she was bathing, fortune, which loves to do strange and unexpected things, procured for her something worthy not of her judgment but of her beauty. For as she was bathing and her maids were guarding her clothing, an eagle swooped down, snatched one of her sandals, and went off; and it carried it to Memphis, where Psammitichus was sitting in judgment, and dropped the sandal into his lap. Psammitichus, marvelling at the shape of the sandal and the grace of its workmanship and at what the bird had done, ordered the woman whose sandal it was to be sought throughout all Egypt; and finding her, he made her his wife.

34. Dionysius, after the order against Leon, having found him, three times bade the bodyguards lead him away, and three times changed his mind, and at each summons kissed him, weeping and cursing himself for having taken up the sword. At the last he was overcome by fear, and ordered him to be slain, saying: "Leon, it is not possible for you to live."
35. Men learned in nature say that the deer, when it needs purging, eats seseli, and when troubled by the bites of spiders, eats crabs.
36. Olympias sent to Eurydice, the daughter of Philip — she had been born to Philip by an Illyrian woman — hemlock and a noose and a sword; and she chose the noose.

37. Gelon the tyrant of the Syracusans held the establishment of his rule most gently; but some seditious men plotted against him. Learning of this, Gelon called the Syracusans together into an assembly and entered armed, and going through all the good he had done them, he uncovered the plot and stripped off his armour, saying to all: "See, then, I stand before you in a tunic, naked of arms, and I give you to do with me whatever you wish." And the Syracusans admired his judgment, and some even handed over the plotters to him to punish, and gave him the rule. But he allowed even these to be punished by the people. And the Syracusans set up a statue of him in an ungirt tunic; and this was a memorial of his popular rule and a lesson to those who should rule in the age to come.

38. Alcibiades greatly admired Homer, and once, coming to a boys' school, asked for a rhapsody of the Iliad. When the teacher said he had nothing of Homer, he struck him a very hard blow with his knuckles and passed on, showing that the man was uneducated and made the boys such. This man, summoned from Sicily by the Athenians to a capital trial, did not obey, saying: "It is foolish for one who has a lawsuit to seek to escape acquittal when he can escape by flight." When someone said, "Do you not trust your country with the judgment about you?" he said: "Not even my mother; for I fear that, not knowing and missing the truth, she might cast the black pebble instead of the white." So learning that death had been decreed against him by his fellow-citizens, he said: "Let us then show that we are alive," and rushing to the Lacedaemonians he kindled the Decelean war against the Athenians. He used to say that the Lacedaemonians did nothing strange in dying fearlessly in war; for, fleeing the hardship of their laws, they gladly exchanged death for the toils they had. And he was wont, they say, to add of his own doings that he lived the life of the Dioscuri, dying and coming back to life on alternate days; for when he prospered with the people he was thought equal to the gods, but when he fared ill he differed not at all from the dead.
39. When someone reproached Ephialtes the general with his poverty, he said: "And why do you not mention the other thing, that I am just?"

40. As a Persian gold necklace lay on the ground, Themistocles, standing by his son, said: "Will you not pick up this find, boy?" — pointing to the necklace — "for you are surely not Themistocles." When the Athenians once dishonoured him, then summoned him again to office, he said: "I do not praise such men, who use the same vessel for chamber-pot and wine-jug." To Eurybiades the Lacedaemonian he said something contrary, and Eurybiades raised his staff against him. And he said: "Strike, but listen." For he knew that what he was about to say would benefit the common good.
41. When one of those about to die with Phocion was lamenting, Phocion said: "What, Thudippus, are you not content to die with Phocion?"

42. Epaminondas was on trial for his life, having returned from Laconia, for having added four months to his Boeotarchy contrary to the law. He bade his fellow-magistrates lay the blame on him as having been compelled, but he himself, coming forward into the court, said he had no words better than his deeds; if otherwise, he asked them to put him to death, but to inscribe on the pillar that Epaminondas had compelled the Thebans against their will to burn Laconia, which had been unravaged for five hundred years, to found Messene after two hundred and thirty years, to organize and gather the Arcadians into one, and to restore to the Greeks their independence. And the judges, out of respect, acquitted him. As he returned from the court, a little Maltese dog fawned on him. So he said to those present: "This creature repays me thanks for a kindness, but the Thebans, having often been well treated by me, have condemned me to death."

43. Timotheus the Athenian general was believed to be fortunate; and they used to say that fortune was the cause, and Timotheus the cause of nothing, mocking him on the stage. And the painters depicted him asleep, and then, hovering over his head, Fortune standing and drawing the cities into a net. When someone asked Themistocles in what he had most delighted in his life, he answered: "To see the theatre at Olympia turning toward me as I passed into the stadium."

44. Themistocles and Aristides the son of Lysimachus had the same guardians, and for this reason they were reared together and educated under a common teacher. Yet they were at variance even while still boys, and the rivalry remained with them from earliest youth to extreme old age.
45. Dionysius killed his mother with poisons; and though able to save his brother Leptines in the sea-battle, he looked on while he perished.

46. Patrae is a city of Achaea. A boy among them bought a small snake and reared it with much care. When it grew, he talked to it as to one who heard, and played with it and slept with it. When the snake reached its greatest size, it was driven by the citizens into the wilderness. Later the boy, having become a young man, was returning from some spectacle, and fell among robbers with his companions; and when a cry arose, behold the snake. And it scattered some, and killed others, and saved him."

1. Aristotle the son of Nicomachus, a wise man both in being so and in seeming so, when someone took from him the honours that had been decreed him at Delphi, wrote to Antipater about these matters thus: "Concerning the honours decreed me at Delphi and of which I have now been deprived, I am so disposed as neither to care greatly about them nor to care nothing at all." This would not be love of glory, nor would I myself condemn any such thing in Aristotle, but, being right-minded, he thought it was not the same thing not to receive some honour and, having received it, to be deprived of it. For the one, not to attain it, is no great matter; but the painful thing is to attain it and then to be robbed of it.
2. Agesilaus praised those of the barbarians who broke their oaths, because, having made the gods their enemies by their perjuries, they made them friends and allies to himself.

3. Timotheus the son of Conon said the best thing of all against Aristophon of the deme Azenia. For since Aristophon was a spendthrift, Timotheus touched him most bitterly, saying: "He for whom nothing is enough — for that man nothing is shameful."

4. Aristides the Locrian, bitten by a Tartessian weasel and dying, said that it would have been much more pleasant to him to die bitten by a lion or a leopard, if indeed death needed some pretext, and that by such a beast — bearing, as it seems to me, the disgrace of the bite much harder than death itself.

5. The Athenians did not make use only of those of their own citizens who were fit for office and command, but they chose foreigners too and entrusted public affairs to them, if indeed they judged them to be good men and fit for such things. Apollodorus of Cyzicus they often chose as general, though he was a foreigner, and Heracleides of Clazomenae; for having shown that they were men worth mentioning, they were then not deemed unworthy to rule the Athenians. And for these things one must praise the city, which did not sacrifice the truth to its citizens, but gave honour even to those who did not belong by birth, but through virtue were worthy to be honoured.

6. Aristippus seemed to speak very forcibly in counselling men neither to be distressed over things past nor to be anxious beforehand over things to come; for such conduct is a sign of cheerfulness and a proof of a serene mind. He bade them keep their thought on the day, and again on that part of the day in which each man is either doing something or planning it. For he said that the present alone is ours, and neither what is past nor what is expected; for the one has perished, and the other is uncertain whether it will be.

7. This is a Lacedaemonian law, and the law says these things. That no Lacedaemonian should be seen more unmanly in colour, or have more bulk of body than the exercises warrant; for the one was taken to confess idleness, the other not to confess a man. It was added to the law that every ten days, without fail, the youths should present themselves naked before the ephors in public. And if they were well-knit and vigorous, and as it were carved and chiselled by their exercises, they were praised; but if any of their limbs was flabby or too soft, with fat swelling and growing on them through indolence, then they were beaten and chastised. And the ephors made it their care each day to busy themselves about their dress, whether every part of it fell short of the fitting order. And there had to be cooks in Lacedaemon of meat only; but whoever knew anything beyond this was driven out of Sparta, like the purgings of the sick. These same men brought down Naucleides the son of Polybiades, who had grown over-fleshed and over-fat in body through luxury, into the assembly of the spectators, and threatened him with the penalty of exile, unless he should reform for the future the life he then lived, which was blameworthy and Ionian rather than Laconian; for they said that his appearance and the condition of his body brought shame both on Lacedaemon and on the laws.

8. Polyclitus made two statues at the same time, the one to please the crowd, the other according to the rule of his art. He pleased the many in this way. For each of those who came in, he changed and reshaped something, yielding to each man's suggestion. So he set out both; and the one was praised by all, but the other was laughed at. Taking them up, then, Polyclitus said: "But this one, which you blame, you made; and this one, which you admire, I made." Hippomachus the flute-teacher, when a pupil of his playing the flute made a mistake in his playing but was praised by those present, struck him with his rod and said: "You played badly; for these men would not have praised you otherwise."

9. Xenocrates of Chalcedon, when mocked unkindly by Plato, never grew indignant, they say; and to the man who urged him on about it, that he might answer Plato something, he very sensibly silenced the man, saying: "But this is good for me."

10. The Athenians chose Demades to be general in preference to Phocion. He, preferred and proud of it, came to Phocion and said: "Lend me the dirty cloak you used to wear during your generalship." And Phocion said: "You will never lack for anything dirty, so long as you are such as you are."

11. Philiscus once said to Alexander: "Care for your reputation, but do not be a plague and a great disease, but health." He meant that to rule by force and harshly, and to take cities and destroy peoples, is the work of a plague, but to take thought for the health and safety of one's subjects is the good work of peace.

12. The king of the Persians, when travelling, that he might not be idle, used to carry a little linden-wood board and a little knife, that he might whittle it. And these the royal hands made; for he had neither book nor thought, that he might read something serious and worthy, or plan something noble and worth mention.

13. Agathon used many antitheses often. When someone, as if correcting him, wished to remove them from his dramas, he said: "But you, my good man, do not realize that you are obliterating Agathon out of Agathon." So proud was he of these, and he thought that this was his tragedy.

14. Someone gave Stratonicus the harper a lavish welcome; and he was overjoyed at the invitation, for he happened to have no lodging, having come to a foreign land. So he warmly embraced the man for the readiness of his sharing his roof. But when he saw one man coming in, and another, and that the man's house was in a manner open and unclosed to all who chose to lodge there, then Stratonicus said to his attendant: "Let us go away from here, boy; for it seems we have a wood-pigeon instead of a dove, having found an inn instead of a house."

15. A story went round saying that the discourses of Socrates were like the paintings of Pauson. For Pauson the painter, having undertaken from someone to paint a horse rolling, painted it running. When the man who had commissioned the picture was indignant, as it was painted contrary to the agreement, the painter answered: "Turn the picture round, and the running horse will be rolling for you." So too Socrates did not converse plainly. If, at any rate, one turned his words round, they were perfectly correct. And the reason was that he did not wish to make himself hateful to those with whom he conversed, and for this reason he made his words riddling and oblique.

16. Hipponicus the son of Callias wished to set up a statue as a dedication to his country. When someone advised him to have the statue made by Polyclitus, he said he would not attend to such a dedication, the glory of which would belong not to the dedicator but to the maker. For it was plain that those who saw the work would admire Polyclitus and not him.

17. Socrates said that Archelaus spent four hundred minae on his house, hiring Zeuxis of Heracleia to decorate it, but nothing on himself. Therefore those who wished to see the house came from afar with great eagerness; but for Archelaus's own sake no one journeyed to Macedon, unless he should persuade and lure someone with money — by which a man of worth would not be won.

18. A man of Chios, angry with his servant, said: "I will not throw you into the mill, but I will take you to Olympia." For he thought, naturally, it was a far harsher punishment for that man to be roasted by the sun's rays while watching at Olympia than to grind, handed over to the mill.

19. Archytas was temperate in other ways, and indeed he guarded against unseemly words. When once he was forced to say something improper, he was not overcome, but kept silent about it, and wrote it upon the wall, showing what he was forced to say, yet not forced to say it.

20. A Sybarite man, a tutor — for indeed, along with the other Sybarites, these too lived in luxury — when the boy he was leading along the road came upon a dried fig and picked it up, rebuked him most severely; but most ludicrously he himself snatched the find from the boy and gobbled it down. When I read this in Sybaritic histories, I laughed; and I gave it to memory, not grudging out of love of mankind that another too should laugh.
21. There was a certain Oeagrus, a poet after Orpheus and Musaeus, who is said to have been the first to sing the Trojan War, having taken up a very great subject and ventured upon it.

22. A certain tyrant, Tryzus, wishing to root out conspiracies and plots against himself, ordered the inhabitants that no one should converse with anyone, neither in public nor in private. And the thing was impossible and grievous. So they outwitted the tyrant's command, and nodded to one another and made gestures to one another, and looked now fiercely and again calmly and cheerfully; and at sorrowful and incurable things each of them was plainly knit of brow, showing to his neighbour the affliction of his soul from his face. This too troubled the tyrant, and he believed that even their silence would surely breed him some harm, through the variety of their gestures. So he put a stop to this too. One of those distressed at the impossibility of their plight, and chafing, and thirsting to dissolve the monarchy, came to the marketplace, then stood and wept with many and abundant tears. So the crowd stood round him and gathered about, and they too were seized with lamentation. News came to the tyrant that none of them used the nod any longer, but that tears were now in fashion among them. And he, eager to put a stop to this too — not only condemning the tongue to slavery, nor the nods alone, but now shutting off from the eyes too their natural freedom — came as fast as his feet would carry him with his bodyguards, that he might check the tears. But no sooner had they seen him than, snatching the weapons of the bodyguards, they killed the tyrant.

23. Cleinias was a man earnest in character, and a Pythagorean in his wisdom. Whenever he was provoked to anger and perceived himself being carried away to wrath, at once, before his anger was full and it became plain how he was disposed, he tuned his lyre and played it. To those who asked the reason he answered fittingly: "I am calming myself." And it seems to me that Achilles too in the Iliad, who sang to the lyre and brought to his own memory through the music the glories of men of old, was lulling his wrath; for, being musical, he took the lyre first from the spoils.

24. They despised wealth and showed greatness of soul, seeing their fellow-citizens in poverty while they themselves were rich: in Corinth Theocles and Thrasonides, and in Mytilene Praxis. And they advised others too to lighten for the destitute the constraint of poverty. When they could not persuade them, they at least remitted the debts owed to themselves, and they profited not in money but in their very lives; for those who were not released, attacking their creditors, putting forward the weapons of their wrath and the most reasonable plea, the irresistible compulsion of their straits, killed the moneylenders.

25. The Chians once fell into faction with one another, suffering most manfully this most grievous disease. So a man among them, of a statesmanlike nature, said to his companions who were eager to expel all their opponents: "By no means; but since we have prevailed, let us leave some behind, that as time goes on, having no rivals, we may not begin to make war on ourselves." And in saying this he persuaded them; for he seemed to speak well, since he spoke thus.

26. Antagoras the poet abused Arcesilaus of the Academy, having fallen out with him, and that too in the marketplace; but he, very high-mindedly, where he saw the most people gathered, there he walked along conversing, that the abuser might disgrace himself before more. So those who heard turned away and charged Antagoras with madness.

27. I praise most of all those who, anticipating the evils that are springing up, cut them off before they take hold of any strength. Agesilaus, at any rate, advised that those who gathered by night during the invasion of the Thebans be put to death without trial.

28. Someone reproached the orator Pytheas that he was a bad man. He did not deny it — for his conscience would not let him; but he answered this, that of those who had taken part in public life at Athens he had been bad for the shortest time — being proud, evidently, that he had not been such throughout, and thinking he did no wrong, since he did not compare himself with the most wicked. But this was foolish of Pytheas; for not only is he who does wrong bad, but also he who thinks of doing wrong, in my judgment.

29. Lysander brought money to Lacedaemon and taught the Lacedaemonians to break the god's command, which ordered that Sparta should be untrodden by gold and silver. Some of the right-minded, then, tried to prevent it, still keeping a Laconian spirit worthy of Lycurgus and of the Pythian god; but those who admitted the money were discredited, and their original virtue little by little gave way.

30. Hanno the Carthaginian through luxury did not deign to remain within the bounds of men, but devised to have reports sown abroad about himself greater than accorded with the nature he had been allotted. For having bought very many singing-birds, he reared them in darkness, teaching them one lesson to say: "Hanno is a god." And when those birds, hearing this one phrase, had mastered it, he let them loose, one this way and one that, thinking that the song about himself would spread abroad through the birds. But they, once they had set their wings free and gained their liberty and come to the habits natural to them, sang their own songs and made the music of birds, bidding a long farewell to Hanno and the lessons learned in slavery.

31. Ptolemy, called Tryphon — for this they called him from his way of life — when a beautiful woman wished to meet with him, said: "My sister has forbidden me to receive a proposal from a beautiful woman." And she, very unabashed and fittingly, said: "Could you receive one from a beautiful man?" And he, hearing it, praised her.

32. A Lacedaemonian man, Timandridas by name, going abroad, left his son as caretaker of his house. Then, returning some time later and finding that the son had made the estate greater than he had left it, he said that the son was wronging many — gods and kinsmen and guests; for the surplus of these things is spent upon them by free men. But to appear poor while living and to be found rich at death — this is the most shameful of things among men.

33. Plato was discoursing on certain matters, and Diogenes, who was present, paid little heed to him. So the son of Ariston was indignant at this and said: "Listen to the discourse, dog." And he, in no way disturbed, said: "But I have not gone back there whence I was sold, as dogs do" — hinting at Plato's journey to Sicily. And Plato, they say, was wont to say of Diogenes that this man was a Socrates gone mad.

34. The Egyptians say that they were instructed in their laws by Hermes; thus each people chooses to glorify what is their own. The judges in old times among the Egyptians were the priests. The eldest of these was their head, and judged all. And he had to be the most just of men and the most unsparing. He wore too an image of sapphire stone about his neck, and the image was called Truth. But I should think it right that the judge should carry Truth not made of stone and fashioned, but should have her in his very soul.
35. Lais was also called the Axe. This surname convicted her of the savagery of her character, and that she charged much, and still more from foreigners, since they departed sooner.

36. One may laugh at those who are proud because of their fathers and their ancestors, seeing that we do not know the father of Marius, yet we admire him for his deeds; and so too with Cato and Servius and Hostilius and Romulus.

37. I love to look neither at the statues which the plastic art shows us, nor at the images, idly; for there is something wise in the handiwork even in these. And one can recognize many other things in them, and among them this. None of the Muses did any painter or sculptor ever prove able to present to us with most false and counterfeit and alien forms of the daughters of Zeus. Or who was ever so madly daring a craftsman as to make them armed? This confirms that the life among the Muses ought to be at once peaceful and gentle and worthy of them.

38. Of Epaminondas the Theban I know many other fine things, and among them this. He used to say to Pelopidas that he should not leave the marketplace before he had won over some younger man as a friend to the older.

39. The king of the Persians — for I wish to tell you something cheerful too — dipping a crown in perfume — and the crown was woven of roses — sent it to Antalcidas, who was on an embassy to him for peace. And he said: "I accept the gift and praise the kindness, but you have destroyed the scent of the roses and the fragrance of nature through the counterfeit of art."

40. Alexander the tyrant of Pherae was thought to be among the most savage of men. When Theodorus the tragic poet was acting Merope very passionately, he burst into tears and then rose up and left the theatre. Excusing himself, he said to Theodorus that he had gone not out of contempt or disdain for him, but out of shame, that he should be able to pity the sufferings of actors, but not those of his own citizens.

41. Apollodorus, who drank the most wine of men, did not conceal his own vice, nor did he try to cloak his drunkenness and the evils that came from it, but, kindled and inflamed by the wine, he became more murderous, having, besides his nature, the drink too as a stimulus.

42. Xenocrates the companion of Plato said that it makes no difference whether one sets one's feet or one's eyes in another's house; for he sins in the same way who looks at places where he ought not, and who passes into places where he ought not.

43. A certain Ptolemy — which one he was, let it pass — sat at dice and kept gaming; then one standing by him read out the names of those condemned and added their sentences, that the king might mark which were worthy of death. But Berenice his wife, taking the document from the page, then would not allow it to be read through entirely any more, saying that one ought to give very careful thought concerning a man's life and not be at play while doing so; for the fall of the dice and the fall of human lives were not alike. At this Ptolemy was pleased, and never afterward, while gaming, did he hear a man's judgment.

44. A Laconian youth bought a piece of land very cheaply; then he was brought before the magistrates and fined. And the cause of the condemnation was this, that being young he loved gain too keenly. For it was among the most manly traits of the Lacedaemonians, this too: to be arrayed not only against enemies but also against money.

45. Among the women of the Greeks we praise Penelope, Alcestis, and the wife of Protesilaus; among the Romans, Cornelia and Porcia and Caestilia. I could have named others too, but I do not wish to name few of the Greeks and flood the rest with the names of the Romans, lest anyone should think I am gratifying myself because of my country.

46. The Magnesians who dwell along the Maeander, when they were at war with the Ephesians, each of the cavalrymen brought with him as fellow-soldier a hunting-dog and a javelin-throwing servant. And when they had to engage, then the dogs, leaping forward, threw the enemy's array into confusion, being fearful and savage and implacable to meet; and the servants, leaping forward before their masters, hurled their javelins. And so, upon the disorder caused first by the dogs, the deeds of the servants too took effect. Then, in the third place, the men themselves advanced.

47. Zeuxis of Heracleia painted Helen. So Nicomachus the painter was struck by the picture, and was plainly amazed at the painting. Someone, then, coming up, asked him what had come over him that he so admired the art. And he said: "You would not have asked me, had you possessed my eyes." And I would say this of words too: but only if one has educated ears, just as the craftsmen have skilled eyes.

48. Philip, taking the sons of the most esteemed men in Macedon, kept them about his own service, in no way, they say, insulting them or making them cheap, but on the contrary training them to endurance and making them ready to do what was needful. But toward those of them who were luxurious and slack at what was commanded he was, they say, hostile. At any rate he flogged Aphthonetus, because, leaving his post, he turned off the road, being thirsty, and went into an innkeeper's. And he killed Archedamus, because, though Philip had ordered him to keep himself in his armour, he stripped it off; for he had hoped, through flattery and fawning, to win over the king, being a man too weak to resist gain."
